title: The eMudhra fix lives in your Go binary, not in your Docker image
summary:
On October 19, Go shipped two security releases: 1.27.3 and 1.26.10. The fix touches a single package, crypto/x509. I rebuilt one of my Go services on the same Docker image as before. Go's own scanner still found the flaw.

TL;DR: the eMudhra fix is a list of eight banned keys, written into the code of crypto/x509. That list is compiled into your binary. Updating the base image or the system certificates does not add it. You have to rebuild with Go 1.27.3 or 1.26.10, then redeploy. If your Dockerfile still builds with Go 1.25, rebuilding changes nothing: that version gets no more fixes.

Versions and source status: snapshot as of October 31, 2026. Check the latest fixes before deploying.

This article is for Go developers and for teams that ship Go services in containers.

What happened with eMudhra

eMudhra is a certificate authority. Most browsers and operating systems accept its certificates.

On October 17, Mozilla blocked eight of its intermediate certificates in Firefox. An intermediate certificate is signed by the root. It is the one that then signs website certificates.

The private keys of those eight certificates were very weak. They could be recovered in microseconds. With one of those keys, anyone can sign a TLS certificate for any domain. They can then sit between your service and the API it calls, and read the traffic.

Go shipped its fix two days later. It was the project's first security release on the "URGENT" track. Usually the team announces a security fix three to seven days before it ships. This time it shipped with no advance notice.

My lab: the same service, three binaries

Only the last two rows compare the same code with two compilers. The April binary is a historical reference.

One of my projects has about ten Go services. They all declare go 1.25.0 in their go.mod. Their Dockerfile builds with golang:1.25-bookworm. It then copies the binary into a distroless image.

I ran one of those services through govulncheck. It is Go's official tool for finding known vulnerabilities. With -mode=binary, it analyzes a compiled binary directly.

In Go's database, the eMudhra flaw is GO-2026-6809. It is still there with Go 1.25.14, and for a good reason: that version never got the fix.

I checked Docker Hub. The golang:1.25-bookworm image is the same as golang:1.25.14-bookworm. It has not changed since August 19.

Go's release policy explains why. Each major release is supported until two newer ones exist. Go 1.27 shipped on August 19. So Go 1.25 gets no fixes at all anymore. With my Dockerfile, rebuilding a hundred times fixes nothing.

The 13 vulnerabilities left with Go 1.27.3 come from my dependencies: golang.org/x/net, golang.org/x/text, gRPC, pgx and OpenTelemetry. Rebuilding fixes the standard library. Modules are updated separately, with go get and tests. I covered that part in my article on the Go supply chain.

The fix is a list, compiled into your binary

I opened the Go 1.27.3 source. The fix adds a table to crypto/x509/verify.go:

// distrustedSPKIHashes contains hashes of SPKIs from certificates which
// we don't consider to be trustworthy. We use these hashes to filter out
// chains returned by Verify
var distrustedSPKIHashes = map[string]struct{}{
    "ebed6475c2c2d80fcb199f3fe8dd6e6b3ce60b77eb15d4e42c3dec0c6f5b5105": {},
    "49dd353dc2b919a3770645117d0e60c16115e7d1bc259eefe734b00ea434fe5f": {},
    // ... six more hashes
}

Each line is the SHA-256 hash of a public key. Verify builds the possible certificate chains. It drops every chain that contains one of those keys. If no chain is left, the TLS connection fails.

Here is the key point. Go compiles its standard library into every binary. So this table lives inside your executable, not on the server's disk.

Updating the ca-certificates package in your image does not bring it in. That package holds root certificates. It cannot exclude an intermediate certificate. The Go team says it in its post: Linux has no system mechanism to revoke an intermediate. That is why it shipped an urgent release.

On Linux, Go checks certificates itself. That covers almost all of your containers. A binary built with an older version still accepts those eight keys.

Nobody watched the line that picks the compiler

Those services do have Dependabot. Dependabot is GitHub's bot that proposes dependency updates. In these repositories, it only watches Go modules, and only my shared internal module.

So the FROM golang:1.25-bookworm line is watched by nothing. The frontend repository watches its Docker images. So does the Keycloak one. The Go services do not.

I also found three Go versions in the same project. My CI runner image ships Go 1.25.8 for the tests. The Dockerfile builds with Go 1.25.14 today. The binary left on my laptop came from Go 1.25.0. The tests pass. They say nothing about the version that built the image.

The lesson is simple. The compiler version is a dependency. It needs watching like the others.

Check what runs, not what is written

For comparable scans, save the date, govulncheck version, commit and build flags. The vulnerability database changes. My lab totals are not expected results for your future scans.

date -u +%FT%TZ
govulncheck -version
git rev-parse HEAD

Your go.mod gives a minimum version. It does not say what built your binary. To find out, ask the binary itself:

go version -m ./my-service | head -1
# ./my-service: go1.25.14

A distroless image usually has no shell. An executable it contains can still run directly. For this check, copy the binary out:

docker create --name check registry/my-service:tag
docker cp check:/my-service ./my-service
docker rm check
govulncheck -mode=binary ./my-service

govulncheck exits with code 3 when it finds a vulnerability. A CI step that runs it fails on its own.

One detail surprised me. My Dockerfile builds with -ldflags="-s -w". That option strips the symbol table from the binary. But govulncheck uses it to know which functions are present. Without it, the tool reports more broadly.

On the same code with Go 1.25.14, it reports 52 vulnerabilities instead of 21. The eMudhra flaw still shows up. For a precise result, also run govulncheck ./... on the source code in your CI. Keep binary mode to check the image you ship.

What to change

For Dependabot, a few lines in .github/dependabot.yml are enough:

  - package-ecosystem: docker
    directory: /
    schedule:
      interval: weekly

The checklist

A standard library fix does not exist until your binary is rebuilt.

  • [ ] Run go version -m on the binary of every deployed image
  • [ ] Check that every binary uses at least go1.27.3 or go1.26.10
  • [ ] Search all your Dockerfiles for FROM golang:1.25 and older
  • [ ] Have Dependabot or Renovate watch the docker ecosystem
  • [ ] Run govulncheck in CI, on the source code and on the binary
  • [ ] Align the CI Go version with the image Go version
  • [ ] Rebuild and redeploy the services nobody has touched in a long time
  • [ ] Update your modules separately, with go get and tests

The takeaway

In Go, part of your TLS security lives in your binary. When Go fixes its standard library, your service stays vulnerable until the next build. And if your build image is no longer supported, you never get a build containing the fix.

Open each of your Dockerfiles today and look at the FROM golang line. It is the dependency nobody reviews.

title: Choosing a Self-Hosted Service Desk: A Practitioner’s Decision Guide
summary:
A self-hosted service desk is more than a ticketing application installed on your own infrastructure. Requests still need to move from intake through assignment, escalation, resolution, and useful knowledge capture—and the team operating the system needs to be able to maintain it.

This guide compares nine options by deployment fit, service-management depth, asset and knowledge support, licensing, and day-to-day administration. Verify the specific edition and version before treating a product as self-hosted. If AI is part of your requirements, confirm whether it works within your private environment and can connect to an enterprise-managed model.

Evaluation criteria

Use the same checks for every finalist. A product name or private-cloud option alone does not establish that a specific edition can run on infrastructure your organization operates.

  • Deployment fit: Verify the edition and version, infrastructure requirements, and support for restricted or air-gapped environments if needed.
  • Service workflow depth: Trace a request from intake to assignment, workflow decisions, updates, resolution, and knowledge capture. A ticket list may not cover processes that cross teams or require approvals.
  • Asset tracking: Check whether technicians can use asset records as part of service work, rather than treating inventory as a separate system or checklist item.
  • Operating and licensing fit: Include setup, administration, support, and licensing prerequisites in the comparison. ONES Desk, for example, is an add-on that requires ONES Project; its published annual rate is $42 per named user for 1–500 users, while on-premises ONES has a 100-user minimum. Review Desk pricing terms and on-premises pricing conditions.

Shortlist

  1. ONES.com: Portal requests create project issues representatives can process, update, answer, or assign. Check the 100-user on-premises minimum and paired Desk-and-Project licensing. Desk workflow details · On-premises terms.
  2. ManageEngine ServiceDesk Plus: Compare the self-hosted edition and its ticketing, request, knowledge, and asset workflows with your requirements.
  3. BMC Helix ITSM: Evaluate for complex ITIL-oriented processes, while accounting for implementation effort.
  4. Ivanti Neurons for ITSM: Consider configurable service workflows, but verify the deployment configuration and asset scope.
  5. TOPdesk: Compare request, knowledge, and service processes, and confirm the edition and administration requirements.
  6. GLPI: Evaluate when open-source ITSM and asset inventory matter together; plan for self-hosting and administration.
  7. Znuny: Assess its self-hosted ticket workflow against internal service processes and maintenance capacity.
  8. osTicket: Consider for focused self-hosted support-ticket handling; it is not a substitute for a broad ITSM suite.
  9. SolarWinds Web Help Desk: Compare ticketing and asset workflows, verifying the current self-hosted edition and support model.

Detailed reviews

ONES.com

Product Overview

ONES.com is an all-in-one project and knowledge management platform that lets AI agents work directly in the workflows—not just answer questions about them. For service management with self-hosted deployment, it combines privately deployed work management with ONES Desk, a ticket-management add-on for handling customer requests. ONES On-Premises is deployed within your organization’s infrastructure and supports single-node, cluster, high-availability, and air-gapped deployments (deployment details).

Why It Was Selected

ONES.com stands out for teams that need both customer ticket handling and control over where their service-management environment runs. With ONES Desk, a customer submits a ticket through the portal; the submission creates an issue in the project, where a service representative can update its status, respond, or assign it to another person. That gives the team a concrete path from intake to ownership and response, rather than a portal disconnected from the work used to manage the request (ONES Desk ticket workflow).

The fit also depends on service-desk scope and team size. ONES Desk is sold as an add-on with ONES Project, costs $42 per named user annually for 1–500 users, and is available on-premises; the on-premises subscription has a 100-user minimum (ONES Desk pricing; ONES On-Premises pricing). These terms make the package and minimum commitment visible when you compare operational needs with licensing and administration resources.

Core Capabilities

  • Pain: A customer request arrives without a clear work record. Capability: A portal submission creates an issue that a service representative can process. Result: The request has a trackable work item for follow-up.
  • Pain: The customer needs an update after submitting a ticket. Capability: The representative can change ticket status and respond to the customer. Result: The service interaction progresses through an explicit status and reply.
  • Pain: A request needs attention from someone outside the initial handler. Capability: The representative can assign the ticket to other personnel. Result: Ownership can move to the person responsible for the next action.
  • Pain: Support staff need to manage incoming work as a queue of active records. Capability: Tickets are handled as project issues that representatives can process and update. Result: The team works from service records rather than relying only on the original submission.
  • Pain: A service team must keep its environment within its own infrastructure. Capability: ONES On-Premises supports customer-infrastructure deployment, including single-node, cluster, high-availability, and air-gapped options. Result: The organization can select a deployment configuration aligned with its infrastructure requirements.
  • Pain: Deployment planning must account for scale and operating resources. Capability: The on-premises subscription has a 100-user minimum. Result: The minimum commitment is clear during team-size and budget planning.
  • Pain: Ticket-management costs need to be assessed alongside the underlying platform. Capability: ONES Desk is a named-user add-on purchased with ONES Project, with an annual rate for 1–500 users. Result: Buyers can account for both the service-desk add-on and its required platform purchase.

Pros

  • Customer-infrastructure deployment includes options from single-node to air-gapped configurations.
  • Ticket intake creates project issues that representatives can update, answer, and assign, connecting request handling with accountable work.
  • Published Desk pricing and the on-premises user minimum provide concrete inputs for licensing and scale assessment.

Cons

  • ONES Desk must be purchased with ONES Project, so licensing requires evaluating the combined package.
  • The on-premises subscription has a 100-user minimum, which is a material commitment to include in budget and rollout planning.
  • Escalation is managed through custom workflows, fields, and automation rather than a built-in escalation feature (ONES Desk escalation guidance).

Pricing

ONES On-Premises provides a 30-day free trial for up to 20 users. Paid plans use annual tiered per-seat pricing, with a 100-user minimum. See ONES.com Pricing.

Best For

ONES.com is best for organizations seeking self-hosted ticket handling where customer submissions need to become assigned, updateable work records, and where the team can plan around the on-premises minimum and paired Desk-and-Project licensing. For example, a service representative can receive a portal request, update its status, reply to the customer, and assign follow-up work while the service environment runs within the organization’s infrastructure. That combination makes it a strong option when deployment control and a connected intake-to-response workflow are the deciding requirements.

ManageEngine ServiceDesk Plus

ServiceDesk Plus is an IT service-management and help-desk platform with self-hosted and cloud editions. Assess its incident and request handling, workflow configuration, knowledge functions, and ITIL-oriented processes against a representative request—for example, an access request that must pass through approval.

Trade-offs: Available functions depend on edition and version, so confirm the precise self-hosted offering. Implementation, licensing, administration, and support can require more planning than a basic ticketing setup. Pricing depends on the edition and licensing arrangement; confirm the current terms.

Best fit: IT teams seeking structured request and incident workflows that can support the required service processes, and able to evaluate and operate the chosen edition.

BMC Helix ITSM

BMC Helix ITSM is aimed at enterprise service management and complex IT operations. Evaluate how its request handling, workflows, knowledge practices, and ITIL-oriented processes map to your actual work, including approvals and fulfillment. Treat asset inventory and tracking as separate requirements to verify in the selected configuration.

Trade-offs: Enterprise implementation and licensing can be a substantial commitment. Self-hosted suitability depends on the particular edition and version, so verify deployment, implementation, and support requirements before shortlisting.

Best fit: Organizations with complex service processes, the resources for an enterprise implementation, and requirements that map to the confirmed configuration.

Ivanti Neurons for ITSM

Ivanti Neurons for ITSM is a service-management option to assess for incident and request workflows, knowledge management, and ITIL-oriented practices. Map a real issue—from recording and assignment through resolution—to the edition and deployment you intend to operate. Check whether asset inventory and tracking are included in that configuration.

Trade-offs: Self-hosted availability varies by product configuration and must be confirmed. Licensing, implementation, ongoing administration, asset scope, and support arrangements also need to be checked against available staff and budget.

Best fit: Teams that need structured service workflows and can validate deployment and capability fit for the specific configuration they plan to use.

TOPdesk

TOPdesk provides structured service management for incidents, requests, knowledge, and broader processes such as changes and problems. Its hosted and self-hosted options should be evaluated separately: confirm that the chosen edition can run on your infrastructure, then map its workflows to your service practices.

Trade-offs: A self-hosted installation adds infrastructure and ongoing administration responsibilities. Confirm coverage for the specific ITIL processes you need; pricing depends on the selected arrangement and is not stated here as a fixed public amount.

Best fit: Service teams seeking defined request and service processes that can operate and administer their own deployment.

GLPI

GLPI combines IT service management with asset inventory and tracking. That can keep equipment context close to a support request—for example, when a technician investigates a reported laptop problem. Its open-source option supports self-hosting.

Trade-offs: Open-source software still requires internal capacity to deploy, administer, and maintain. Teams should compare its service-management depth with complex ITIL needs and confirm the support or paid-service arrangement that fits their operations.

Best fit: Organizations that want service requests and asset records in the same operational tool and have the capacity to run it.

Znuny

Znuny is an open-source, self-hosted service desk centered on ticket handling. Staff can capture requests, track progress, and manage responses in a shared queue; technical teams can assess the platform against their own processes and configuration needs.

Trade-offs: Self-hosting places installation, upgrades, security, backups, and administration on your organization. Assess asset inventory, knowledge management, and ITIL process coverage separately rather than assuming a ticket workflow supplies them.

Best fit: Technically capable teams prioritizing self-hosted ticket management and able to maintain the system.

osTicket

osTicket is an open-source help desk that can be self-hosted. Email and web forms can collect requests; agents can organize tickets into queues, assign them, add internal notes, communicate with requesters, and track status. Configurable forms can capture details such as request type or affected device.

Trade-offs: Its focus is support ticketing, not a complete asset inventory or broad ITIL suite. Complex approvals, reporting, or asset lifecycle requirements may need customization or additional systems. The organization is responsible for maintaining a self-hosted installation.

Best fit: Small support teams that need clear request-to-resolution tracking and have the technical capacity to operate the help desk.

SolarWinds Web Help Desk

SolarWinds Web Help Desk combines help-desk ticketing with asset tracking, knowledge management, and reporting. Asset records can provide context while technicians handle a support request, while knowledge and reporting support repeatable answers and operational review.

Trade-offs: It is oriented toward IT help-desk operations, so compare its process depth with broader service-management or complex ITIL requirements. Confirm the current self-hosted edition and plan for infrastructure and administration. Pricing depends on the applicable licensing arrangement.

Best fit: IT teams that need ticket handling and asset tracking together and can operate the required deployment.

Choose by constraints, not feature count

  1. Set the deployment boundary. Record the required infrastructure, edition, and any restricted-network or air-gap constraints. Remove products that cannot meet them.
  2. Walk through a real request. Trace intake, assignment, workflow decisions, updates, knowledge use, asset context, and resolution. Compare the actual steps rather than counting features.
  3. Check operating fit. Include licensing prerequisites, implementation, administration, and support. For ONES.com, account for Desk requiring ONES Project, the $42 annual Desk rate per named user for 1–500 users, and the 100-user on-premises minimum. See Desk pricing and on-premises terms.

Conclusion

ONES.com is worth shortlisting when you need self-hosted portal requests to become work records representatives can process, update, answer, or assign—and your team can meet the 100-user on-premises minimum and paired Desk-and-Project licensing requirements. GLPI is a relevant alternative when open-source ITSM and asset inventory are central. For complex ITIL-oriented processes, evaluate BMC Helix ITSM against your process scope and implementation capacity. For every finalist, verify the exact self-hosted edition and test the same representative request and asset scenario before deciding.

FAQs

How can I tell whether a service-management product is truly self-hosted?

Check the exact edition and version, then confirm that it can be installed on infrastructure your organization operates. A private-cloud offering is not automatically deployment on your own systems.

Which self-hosted option should I evaluate when asset tracking matters?

GLPI is relevant because it combines open-source ITSM with asset inventory. Check how its inventory records support your actual ticket and service workflows.

What should I compare beyond ticket creation?

title: Kubernetes Cookbook Part 8: Persistent Storage That Survives Restarts
summary:
Everything you have run so far in this series shares a dirty secret: when a container dies, its files die with it. A container's filesystem is a whiteboard — easy to write on, wiped clean on restart. That is fine for stateless web servers, but the moment you want a database, an upload folder, or logs that survive a crash, you need real disk. In this part you will cook with Kubernetes storage: you will claim disk without knowing anything about it, watch data survive Pod deletion, learn what access modes and reclaim policies actually mean, and provision a volume by hand to see the machinery up close.

The plain-English mental model is this: a StorageClass is the menu of disk types your cluster offers, a PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) is your order from that menu, and a PersistentVolume (PV) is the actual disk that shows up. One more acronym: CSI, the Container Storage Interface, is the plugin standard that lets Kubernetes talk to any storage system — cloud disks, NFS, local SSDs — without Kubernetes knowing the details of each one. You will never type "CSI" in a YAML file; it just works behind the scenes.

What you need

  • A running local cluster from Part 1 (kind or minikube).
  • Comfort with Pods from Part 2 and Deployments from Part 4.
  • No files to carry over — we create everything fresh in this part.

Recipe 1: Claim disk without thinking

Problem: Your clinerds-demo Pod writes files that vanish every time the Pod restarts. You want a folder that keeps its contents no matter what happens to the Pod.

First, see what is on the menu. Every kind and minikube cluster ships with a default StorageClass:

kubectl get storageclass

NAME                 PROVISIONER                RECLAIMPOLICY   VOLUMEBINDINGMODE   AGE
standard (default)   rancher.io/local-path      Delete          WaitForFirstConsumer 12m

On kind the provisioner is rancher.io/local-path, a small CSI driver that carves directories out of the node's disk. On minikube it is called standard with the k8s.io/minikube-hostpath provisioner. Either way, the (default) marker means you can order disk without naming the menu item.

Create the claim — the order:

# demo-pvc.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: demo-data
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 100Mi

kubectl apply -f demo-pvc.yaml
kubectl get pvc

NAME        STATUS   VOLUME                                     CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   STORAGECLASS   AGE
demo-data   Bound    pvc-7f3a2c1e-9b4d-4e6a-8c5f-2d1b3e9a7f0c   100Mi      RWO            standard       5s

Now mount it into a Pod and write something:

# demo-pod.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: clinerds-demo
spec:
  containers:
    - name: web
      image: hashicorp/http-echo
      args: ["-text=hello from storage"]
      ports:
        - containerPort: 5678
      volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /data
  volumes:
    - name: data
      persistentVolumeClaim:
        claimName: demo-data

kubectl apply -f demo-pod.yaml
kubectl wait --for=condition=ready pod/clinerds-demo --timeout=60s
kubectl exec clinerds-demo -- sh -c 'echo "i was here" > /data/proof.txt'

The proof: kill the Pod, start a fresh one, and check the file.

kubectl delete pod clinerds-demo
kubectl apply -f demo-pod.yaml
kubectl exec clinerds-demo -- cat /data/proof.txt

i was here

How it works: The moment you created the PVC, the default StorageClass's CSI driver dynamically provisioned a real PersistentVolume to match your order — a 100Mi directory on the node — and bound it to your claim. You never wrote a PV manifest; one appeared with a generated pvc-... name. The Pod spec wires the claim into a named volume and mounts that volume at /data inside the container. When the Pod died, only the container's whiteboard filesystem was wiped. The volume lives on the node, and the new Pod mounted the same claim to the same disk. Your data survived because it never lived inside the container at all.

Variations:

  • Mount the same PVC into a Deployment with several replicas and every replica sees the same files — with one big catch, covered in the next recipe.
  • A Pod can mount many claims. Give each volume a unique name and its own mountPath.

Recipe 2: Access modes in plain words

Problem: Your YAML keeps asking for accessModes and you have been copying ReadWriteOnce on faith. You want to know what the choices mean before one bites you.

There are three modes, and they describe how many nodes may use the volume at once, not how many Pods:

  • ReadWriteOnce (RWO) — one node at a time, read and write. The default you almost always want. Cloud disks (EBS, GCE PD) are RWO: a disk can only attach to one machine.
  • ReadOnlyMany (ROX) — many nodes, but read-only. Good for shipping a big reference dataset to many Pods.
  • ReadWriteMany (RWX) — many nodes, read and write. This needs storage that speaks a shared-filesystem protocol, like NFS or a cloud file service. Your laptop's local-path driver cannot do this — it only hands out directories on one node.

Check the modes in play on your cluster:

kubectl get pv,pvc

NAME                          CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   RECLAIM POLICY   STATUS   CLAIM
pvc-7f3a2c1e-...              100Mi      RWO            Delete           Bound    default/demo-data

NAME                              STATUS   VOLUME       CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES
persistentvolumeclaim/demo-data   Bound    pvc-7f3a...  100Mi      RWO

The ACCESS MODES column abbreviates: RWO, ROX, RWX.

How it works: The access mode is a contract between the claim and the volume. A PVC asking for RWO will only bind to a PV that offers RWO. Kubernetes enforces RWO at scheduling time — if a volume is mounted on node A, a Pod using it cannot be scheduled to node B. The classic symptom of hitting this: you scale a Deployment that mounts an RWO volume to two replicas, the second Pod lands on another node, and it sits in ContainerCreating forever with a Multi-Attach error in its events. If you genuinely need many Pods on many nodes writing to one volume, use an RWX-capable StorageClass (NFS, or a managed file service in the cloud) or rethink the design — object storage is often the better answer.

Recipe 3: Reclaim policies — what happens when you let go

Problem: You are about to delete a PVC and you need to know: does the data die with the claim, or can you get it back?

Every PV has a reclaim policy with two useful values:

  • Delete — when the claim is deleted, the volume and the data on it are destroyed. This is the default for dynamically provisioned volumes, including kind's local-path driver.
  • Retain — when the claim is deleted, the volume is kept, flagged as Released, and left alone with data intact.

Demonstrate Retain. Patch your PV (use the name from kubectl get pv):

kubectl patch pv pvc-7f3a2c1e-9b4d-4e6a-8c5f-2d1b3e9a7f0c \
  -p '{"spec":{"persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy":"Retain"}}'

Now delete the Pod and the claim, and look at the volume:

kubectl delete pod clinerds-demo
kubectl delete pvc demo-data
kubectl get pv

NAME                CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   RECLAIM POLICY   STATUS     CLAIM
pvc-7f3a2c1e-...    100Mi      RWO            Retain           Released   default/demo-data

The status is Released, not Available. The volume still remembers its old claim and refuses to bind to anyone new — that is deliberate, so nobody accidentally grabs a disk full of someone else's data. To re-claim it, clear the old claim reference:

kubectl patch pv pvc-7f3a2c1e-9b4d-4e6a-8c5f-2d1b3e9a7f0c \
  -p '{"spec":{"claimRef": null}}'
kubectl get pv   # now shows Available

A fresh PVC can now bind to it and proof.txt is still sitting inside.

How it works: Deleting a PVC never touches data directly — it only ends the claim. The reclaim policy is the PV's last will: Delete tells the provisioner to shred the underlying disk, Retain tells everyone to keep their hands off until a human decides. Released is a safety lock: the volume holds the name of its former claim in spec.claimRef, and until you clear that field, the PV cannot bind again. In production, set Retain on anything you would cry about losing — database volumes are the classic case — so a fat-fingered kubectl delete pvc becomes an annoyance instead of an outage.

When it goes wrong:

  • You patched the PV but the policy still says Delete: kubectl patch typed against the wrong PV name. Re-run kubectl get pv and copy the exact name.
  • After clearing claimRef, your new PVC stays Pending: the new claim probably asks for more storage or a different access mode than the PV offers. Make the request match the volume exactly.

Recipe 4: Static provisioning to see the machinery

Problem: Dynamic provisioning feels like magic, and magic is hard to debug. You want to create a PersistentVolume by hand so the whole lifecycle is visible.

Write the PV yourself. On kind, every Pod runs on a node that is itself a container, and that node has a real filesystem — so a hostPath volume works as our pretend disk:

# manual-pv.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: manual-pv
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: 100Mi
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain
  hostPath:
    path: /tmp/manual-pv
    type: DirectoryOrCreate

Now a claim that matches it — note there is no StorageClass anywhere:

# manual-pvc.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: manual-data
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  storageClassName: ""
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 100Mi

kubectl apply -f manual-pv.yaml
kubectl apply -f manual-pvc.yaml
kubectl get pv,pvc

NAME               CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   RECLAIM POLICY   STATUS   CLAIM
manual-pv          100Mi      RWO            Retain           Bound    default/manual-data

The empty storageClassName: "" is important: it tells Kubernetes "do not dynamically provision anything, only bind me to an existing PV." Without it, the default StorageClass would jump in and make you a second volume.

How it works: This is static provisioning: an admin (you) creates the PV first, and a PVC binds to it only if capacity, access modes, and storage class line up. That binding logic is the same one dynamic provisioning uses — the only difference is who writes the PV, a human or a CSI driver. Binding is one-to-one: a bound PV serves exactly one claim until released. Now the honest warning: hostPath means "a directory on whichever node the Pod lands on." Reschedule the Pod to another node and your data is not there. Treat this recipe as an X-ray of how PVs and PVCs fit together, never as production storage.

Recipe 5: Day-2 storage chores

Problem: The volume works. Now you need the boring operational skills: seeing how full it is, growing it, and deleting things in the right order.

Check real usage from inside the Pod:

kubectl exec clinerds-demo -- df -h /data

Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/vda1        75G  3.2G   72G   5% /data

There is your mount, attached at /data, with the node's real filesystem behind it. (The local-path driver does not enforce the 100Mi request — the size is a reservation for scheduling, not a hard quota. Cloud disks do enforce it, because the request becomes the actual disk size.)

Clean up in the right order when you are done:

kubectl delete pod clinerds-demo
kubectl delete pvc demo-data
kubectl get pv   # Delete policy: gone. Retain policy: Released, yours to handle.

How it works: df -h works because a mounted volume is just a directory inside the container's filesystem view — standard Linux tools see it like any other mount. The cleanup order is the gotcha that bites beginners: always delete the PVC first and let the reclaim policy deal with the PV. If you delete a bound PV first, it hangs in Terminating because the claim still points at it, and you end up force-patching finalizers at 2 a.m. Claim first, volume second — the policy does the rest.

Variations:

  • Volume expansion: if the StorageClass has allowVolumeExpansion: true (check with kubectl get sc standard -o yaml), you can grow a volume in place by editing the PVC: kubectl edit pvc demo-data, raise spec.resources.requests.storage, save, and the filesystem grows without downtime. Shrinking is never allowed.
  • The local-path provisioner ignores allowVolumeExpansion, so test expansion on a cloud cluster or minikube with a driver that supports it.

Where to go next

You can now hand any stateless app a disk that outlives it. The next natural step is the app that is all about its disk: databases and queues that need stable names, stable storage, and ordered startup. That is exactly what StatefulSets are for, and it is where we cook next in Part 9: StatefulSets. For the full reference on everything in this part — phases, binding rules, and every field on the PV and PVC objects — keep the official Persistent Volumes documentation bookmarked. The whole menu is at the series index.

Problem: Your clinerds-demo Pod writes files that vanish every time the Pod restarts. You want a folder that keeps its contents no matter what happens to the Pod.

First, see what is on the menu. Every kind and minikube cluster ships with a default StorageClass:

kubectl get storageclass

NAME                 PROVISIONER                RECLAIMPOLICY   VOLUMEBINDINGMODE   AGE
standard (default)   rancher.io/local-path      Delete          WaitForFirstConsumer 12m

On kind the provisioner is rancher.io/local-path, a small CSI driver that carves directories out of the node's disk. On minikube it is called standard with the k8s.io/minikube-hostpath provisioner. Either way, the (default) marker means you can order disk without naming the menu item.

Create the claim — the order:

# demo-pvc.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: demo-data
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 100Mi

kubectl apply -f demo-pvc.yaml
kubectl get pvc

NAME        STATUS   VOLUME                                     CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   STORAGECLASS   AGE
demo-data   Bound    pvc-7f3a2c1e-9b4d-4e6a-8c5f-2d1b3e9a7f0c   100Mi      RWO            standard       5s

Now mount it into a Pod and write something:

# demo-pod.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: clinerds-demo
spec:
  containers:
    - name: web
      image: hashicorp/http-echo
      args: ["-text=hello from storage"]
      ports:
        - containerPort: 5678
      volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /data
  volumes:
    - name: data
      persistentVolumeClaim:
        claimName: demo-data

kubectl apply -f demo-pod.yaml
kubectl wait --for=condition=ready pod/clinerds-demo --timeout=60s
kubectl exec clinerds-demo -- sh -c 'echo "i was here" > /data/proof.txt'

The proof: kill the Pod, start a fresh one, and check the file.

kubectl delete pod clinerds-demo
kubectl apply -f demo-pod.yaml
kubectl exec clinerds-demo -- cat /data/proof.txt

i was here

How it works: The moment you created the PVC, the default StorageClass's CSI driver dynamically provisioned a real PersistentVolume to match your order — a 100Mi directory on the node — and bound it to your claim. You never wrote a PV manifest; one appeared with a generated pvc-... name. The Pod spec wires the claim into a named volume and mounts that volume at /data inside the container. When the Pod died, only the container's whiteboard filesystem was wiped. The volume lives on the node, and the new Pod mounted the same claim to the same disk. Your data survived because it never lived inside the container at all.

Variations:

  • Mount the same PVC into a Deployment with several replicas and every replica sees the same files — with one big catch, covered in the next recipe.
  • A Pod can mount many claims. Give each volume a unique name and its own mountPath.

Recipe 2: Access modes in plain words

Problem: Your YAML keeps asking for accessModes and you have been copying ReadWriteOnce on faith. You want to know what the choices mean before one bites you.

There are three modes, and they describe how many nodes may use the volume at once, not how many Pods:

  • ReadWriteOnce (RWO) — one node at a time, read and write. The default you almost always want. Cloud disks (EBS, GCE PD) are RWO: a disk can only attach to one machine.
  • ReadOnlyMany (ROX) — many nodes, but read-only. Good for shipping a big reference dataset to many Pods.
  • ReadWriteMany (RWX) — many nodes, read and write. This needs storage that speaks a shared-filesystem protocol, like NFS or a cloud file service. Your laptop's local-path driver cannot do this — it only hands out directories on one node.

Check the modes in play on your cluster:

kubectl get pv,pvc

NAME                          CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   RECLAIM POLICY   STATUS   CLAIM
pvc-7f3a2c1e-...              100Mi      RWO            Delete           Bound    default/demo-data

NAME                              STATUS   VOLUME       CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES
persistentvolumeclaim/demo-data   Bound    pvc-7f3a...  100Mi      RWO

The ACCESS MODES column abbreviates: RWO, ROX, RWX.

How it works: The access mode is a contract between the claim and the volume. A PVC asking for RWO will only bind to a PV that offers RWO. Kubernetes enforces RWO at scheduling time — if a volume is mounted on node A, a Pod using it cannot be scheduled to node B. The classic symptom of hitting this: you scale a Deployment that mounts an RWO volume to two replicas, the second Pod lands on another node, and it sits in ContainerCreating forever with a Multi-Attach error in its events. If you genuinely need many Pods on many nodes writing to one volume, use an RWX-capable StorageClass (NFS, or a managed file service in the cloud) or rethink the design — object storage is often the better answer.

Recipe 3: Reclaim policies — what happens when you let go

Problem: You are about to delete a PVC and you need to know: does the data die with the claim, or can you get it back?

Every PV has a reclaim policy with two useful values:

  • Delete — when the claim is deleted, the volume and the data on it are destroyed. This is the default for dynamically provisioned volumes, including kind's local-path driver.
  • Retain — when the claim is deleted, the volume is kept, flagged as Released, and left alone with data intact.

Demonstrate Retain. Patch your PV (use the name from kubectl get pv):

kubectl patch pv pvc-7f3a2c1e-9b4d-4e6a-8c5f-2d1b3e9a7f0c \
  -p '{"spec":{"persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy":"Retain"}}'

Now delete the Pod and the claim, and look at the volume:

kubectl delete pod clinerds-demo
kubectl delete pvc demo-data
kubectl get pv

NAME                CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   RECLAIM POLICY   STATUS     CLAIM
pvc-7f3a2c1e-...    100Mi      RWO            Retain           Released   default/demo-data

The status is Released, not Available. The volume still remembers its old claim and refuses to bind to anyone new — that is deliberate, so nobody accidentally grabs a disk full of someone else's data. To re-claim it, clear the old claim reference:

kubectl patch pv pvc-7f3a2c1e-9b4d-4e6a-8c5f-2d1b3e9a7f0c \
  -p '{"spec":{"claimRef": null}}'
kubectl get pv   # now shows Available

A fresh PVC can now bind to it and proof.txt is still sitting inside.

How it works: Deleting a PVC never touches data directly — it only ends the claim. The reclaim policy is the PV's last will: Delete tells the provisioner to shred the underlying disk, Retain tells everyone to keep their hands off until a human decides. Released is a safety lock: the volume holds the name of its former claim in spec.claimRef, and until you clear that field, the PV cannot bind again. In production, set Retain on anything you would cry about losing — database volumes are the classic case — so a fat-fingered kubectl delete pvc becomes an annoyance instead of an outage.

When it goes wrong:

  • You patched the PV but the policy still says Delete: kubectl patch typed against the wrong PV name. Re-run kubectl get pv and copy the exact name.
  • After clearing claimRef, your new PVC stays Pending: the new claim probably asks for more storage or a different access mode than the PV offers. Make the request match the volume exactly.

Recipe 4: Static provisioning to see the machinery

Problem: Dynamic provisioning feels like magic, and magic is hard to debug. You want to create a PersistentVolume by hand so the whole lifecycle is visible.

Write the PV yourself. On kind, every Pod runs on a node that is itself a container, and that node has a real filesystem — so a hostPath volume works as our pretend disk:

# manual-pv.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: manual-pv
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: 100Mi
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain
  hostPath:
    path: /tmp/manual-pv
    type: DirectoryOrCreate

Now a claim that matches it — note there is no StorageClass anywhere:

# manual-pvc.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: manual-data
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  storageClassName: ""
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 100Mi

kubectl apply -f manual-pv.yaml
kubectl apply -f manual-pvc.yaml
kubectl get pv,pvc

NAME               CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   RECLAIM POLICY   STATUS   CLAIM
manual-pv          100Mi      RWO            Retain           Bound    default/manual-data

The empty storageClassName: "" is important: it tells Kubernetes "do not dynamically provision anything, only bind me to an existing PV." Without it, the default StorageClass would jump in and make you a second volume.

How it works: This is static provisioning: an admin (you) creates the PV first, and a PVC binds to it only if capacity, access modes, and storage class line up. That binding logic is the same one dynamic provisioning uses — the only difference is who writes the PV, a human or a CSI driver. Binding is one-to-one: a bound PV serves exactly one claim until released. Now the honest warning: hostPath means "a directory on whichever node the Pod lands on." Reschedule the Pod to another node and your data is not there. Treat this recipe as an X-ray of how PVs and PVCs fit together, never as production storage.

Recipe 5: Day-2 storage chores

Problem: The volume works. Now you need the boring operational skills: seeing how full it is, growing it, and deleting things in the right order.

Check real usage from inside the Pod:

kubectl exec clinerds-demo -- df -h /data

Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/vda1        75G  3.2G   72G   5% /data

There is your mount, attached at /data, with the node's real filesystem behind it. (The local-path driver does not enforce the 100Mi request — the size is a reservation for scheduling, not a hard quota. Cloud disks do enforce it, because the request becomes the actual disk size.)

Clean up in the right order when you are done:

kubectl delete pod clinerds-demo
kubectl delete pvc demo-data
kubectl get pv   # Delete policy: gone. Retain policy: Released, yours to handle.

How it works: df -h works because a mounted volume is just a directory inside the container's filesystem view — standard Linux tools see it like any other mount. The cleanup order is the gotcha that bites beginners: always delete the PVC first and let the reclaim policy deal with the PV. If you delete a bound PV first, it hangs in Terminating because the claim still points at it, and you end up force-patching finalizers at 2 a.m. Claim first, volume second — the policy does the rest.

Variations:

  • Volume expansion: if the StorageClass has allowVolumeExpansion: true (check with kubectl get sc standard -o yaml), you can grow a volume in place by editing the PVC: kubectl edit pvc demo-data, raise spec.resources.requests.storage, save, and the filesystem grows without downtime. Shrinking is never allowed.
  • The local-path provisioner ignores allowVolumeExpansion, so test expansion on a cloud cluster or minikube with a driver that supports it.

Where to go next

You can now hand any stateless app a disk that outlives it. The next natural step is the app that is all about its disk: databases and queues that need stable names, stable storage, and ordered startup. That is exactly what StatefulSets are for, and it is where we cook next in Part 9: StatefulSets. For the full reference on everything in this part — phases, binding rules, and every field on the PV and PVC objects — keep the official Persistent Volumes documentation bookmarked. The whole menu is at the series index.

title: Kubernetes Cookbook Part 9: StatefulSets for Apps That Remember
summary:
So far in this series, every Pod you have run has been interchangeable. A Deployment does not care if it replaces Pod A with Pod B, because the app inside holds no state of its own. That assumption breaks the moment you run something that remembers: a database, a message queue, a distributed cache. Those apps need a stable name, stable network identity, and storage that belongs to them and nobody else. In this part you will cook with StatefulSets, the workload controller built exactly for apps that remember.

What you need

  • A local cluster (kind or minikube) from Part 1.
  • Working knowledge of Deployments and Services from Part 4 and Part 5.
  • Storage basics from Part 8, especially PersistentVolumeClaims (PVCs). StatefulSets build directly on them.
  • kubectl configured to talk to your cluster.
  • A helper Pod for DNS lookups; we use nicolaka/netshoot below.

Why not just use a Deployment for a database? Two reasons. First, a Deployment gives Pods random names like web-7c9d4f6b8-x1v2t, and the name changes every time the Pod restarts. Database clusters need peers to find each other at a fixed address. Second, a Deployment mounts one shared PVC (or none at all). A database replica must own its own disk, and that disk must survive a Pod being deleted. StatefulSets solve both problems.

Recipe 1: A StatefulSet with a headless Service

Problem: You want three replicas that each get a predictable name and a stable DNS (Domain Name System) entry, so other Pods can reach a specific replica directly.

A StatefulSet always works together with a headless Service — a Service with clusterIP: None. The Service does not load-balance; it only creates DNS records, one per Pod. Create nginx-statefulset.yaml:

apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nginx
  labels:
    app: nginx
spec:
  clusterIP: None
  selector:
    app: nginx
  ports:
    - port: 80
      name: web
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  serviceName: nginx
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nginx
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nginx
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: nginx
          image: nginx:1.27
          ports:
            - containerPort: 80
              name: web
          command:
            - /bin/sh
            - -c
            - |
              echo "Hello from $(hostname)" > /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html
              nginx -g "daemon off;"

Apply it and watch the Pods come up:

kubectl apply -f nginx-statefulset.yaml
kubectl get pods -w -l app=nginx

NAME    READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
web-0   1/1     Running   0          12s
web-1   1/1     Running   0          8s
web-2   1/1     Running   0          4s

Notice the names: web-0, web-1, web-2. The StatefulSet name plus an ordinal, starting at zero. No random suffix. Now verify the per-Pod DNS from a debug Pod:

kubectl run dns-test --rm -it --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- bash
nslookup web-0.nginx.default.svc.cluster.local
curl web-1.nginx.default.svc.cluster.local

Server:    10.96.0.10
Address:   10.96.0.10#53

Name:   web-0.nginx.default.svc.cluster.local
Address: 10.244.0.7

How it works: Every Pod in a StatefulSet gets a DNS record of the form ...svc.cluster.local. The headless Service tells Kubernetes not to allocate a virtual IP for the Service itself. Instead, DNS resolves each Pod name straight to that Pod's IP address. The serviceName field on the StatefulSet is mandatory — it ties the StatefulSet to the headless Service that publishes these records. Each replica prints its own hostname into its index page, so curling each Pod's DNS name returns a different answer. That is the whole point: the replicas are individuals, not clones.

Recipe 2: Per-Pod storage with volumeClaimTemplates

Problem: Each replica needs its own disk, created automatically, and the data must survive the Pod being deleted.

You could not do this with a plain Deployment: one PVC in a Deployment is shared by every replica (or impossible to scale with ReadWriteOnce volumes). StatefulSets add volumeClaimTemplates, a cookie cutter that stamps out one PVC per Pod. Extend your StatefulSet with a template and a mount:

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  serviceName: nginx
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nginx
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nginx
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: nginx
          image: nginx:1.27
          ports:
            - containerPort: 80
              name: web
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /usr/share/nginx/html
  volumeClaimTemplates:
    - metadata:
        name: data
      spec:
        accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
        resources:
          requests:
            storage: 100Mi

Apply it, then write distinct data into each Pod:

kubectl apply -f nginx-statefulset.yaml
kubectl exec web-0 -- sh -c 'echo "data belonging to web-0" > /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html'
kubectl exec web-1 -- sh -c 'echo "data belonging to web-1" > /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html'
kubectl exec web-2 -- sh -c 'echo "data belonging to web-2" > /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html'

Now the interesting part. Delete web-1 and watch what happens:

kubectl delete pod web-1
kubectl get pods -l app=nginx -w
kubectl exec web-1 -- cat /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html

data belonging to web-1

The Pod came back with the same name and its old data. List the PVCs the StatefulSet created for you:

kubectl get pvc

NAME           STATUS   VOLUME     CAPACITY   STORAGECLASS   AGE
data-web-0     Bound    pvc-a1b2   100Mi      standard       5m
data-web-1     Bound    pvc-c3d4   100Mi      standard       5m
data-web-2     Bound    pvc-e5f6   100Mi      standard       5m

How it works: For each Pod, the StatefulSet creates a PVC named - — here data-web-0 and friends. Deleting a Pod does not delete its PVC. When the StatefulSet recreates web-1, it reattaches the existing data-web-1 volume, so the file you wrote is still there. The Pod is disposable; the identity and the disk are not. That pairing of stable name plus stable storage is the core of what a StatefulSet buys you.

Recipe 3: Orderly scaling

Problem: You want to add replicas, but a database cluster must join new members one at a time, not all at once.

StatefulSets scale in strict order. Scale up to five and watch:

kubectl scale statefulset web --replicas=5
kubectl get pods -l app=nginx -w

web-0   1/1     Running   0          20m
web-1   1/1     Running   0          20m
web-2   1/1     Running   0          20m
web-3   1/1     Running   0          6s
web-4   0/1     Pending   0          2s

web-4 does not even start until web-3 is Running and Ready. Now scale back down and watch the reverse:

kubectl scale statefulset web --replicas=3
kubectl get pods -l app=nginx -w

web-4 terminates first, fully, before web-3 is touched. Lowest ordinals are the last to die.

How it works: The default behavior is called OrderedReady. A Pod with ordinal N is only created after N-1 is ready, and Pods are terminated in reverse ordinal order. This matters enormously for clustered software: a new database replica must finish catching up before the next one joins, and shutdown order often matters for graceful leader election.

Variations:

  • If your replicas truly do not depend on each other, set podManagementPolicy: Parallel in the StatefulSet spec. All Pods start and stop at once, trading order for speed.
  • Scaling down does not delete the PVCs of the removed Pods. Scale back up later and the data is still waiting.

Recipe 4: Careful updates with partitions

Problem: You want to roll out a new image slowly, canarying it on one replica before touching the rest.

StatefulSet rolling updates go from the highest ordinal down: web-2 updates first, then web-1, then web-0. The partition field lets you stop partway. Any Pod with an ordinal greater than or equal to the partition gets updated; the rest stay on the old version.

kubectl patch statefulset web --type='json' -p='[
  {"op": "replace", "path": "/spec/updateStrategy/rollingUpdate/partition", "value": 2},
  {"op": "replace", "path": "/spec/template/spec/containers/0/image", "value": "nginx:1.29"}
]'

Delete web-2 to trigger its update (the controller only recreates a Pod above the partition when it is deleted or restarted):

kubectl delete pod web-2
kubectl get pod web-2 -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].image}'

nginx:1.29

Only web-2 moved. If the new version looks healthy, lower the partition to let the rest update:

kubectl patch statefulset web --type='json' \
  -p='[{"op": "replace", "path": "/spec/updateStrategy/rollingUpdate/partition", "value": 0}]'

How it works: With partition 2, the controller treats ordinals 0 and 1 as fenced off. It updates web-2, waits for it to be Ready, and stops. Setting the partition back to 0 resumes the normal ordered rollout. This gives you a built-in canary: the least important replica (by convention, the highest ordinal) takes the risk first. Two other strategies exist for updateStrategy.type: OnDelete, which never touches a Pod until you delete it yourself (full manual control), and the default RollingUpdate you just used.

Recipe 5: The cleanup gotcha

Problem: You are done with the StatefulSet, so you delete it — and your data silently survives.

kubectl delete statefulset web
kubectl delete service nginx
kubectl get pvc

NAME           STATUS   CAPACITY   AGE
data-web-0     Bound    100Mi      1h
data-web-1     Bound    100Mi      1h
data-web-2     Bound    100Mi      1h

The PVCs are still there. This is deliberate: Kubernetes refuses to guess whether your data is safe to destroy. If you are sure you want it gone, delete the PVCs explicitly:

kubectl delete pvc -l app=nginx

(The StatefulSet labels each template-created PVC with the Pod's labels, so -l app=nginx selects them.)

How it works: A StatefulSet owns its Pods but treats PVCs as precious cargo. Deleting the controller orphans the claims rather than cascading the deletion. On a real cluster with real data, that one design choice has saved many careers.

Variations and warnings:

  • Running PostgreSQL or Redis by hand with raw StatefulSets is a great way to learn, and a rough way to run production. Real databases on Kubernetes are usually managed by Operators — higher-level controllers that handle failover, backups, and upgrades for you. Look at CloudNativePG for PostgreSQL or the Bitnami Helm charts for a batteries-included start.
  • Never point two StatefulSets at the same PVC naming scheme; you will get confusing mount conflicts.

Where to go next

You now know how to run apps that remember: stable names, per-Pod storage, ordered scaling, and careful updates. In the final part of the series, you will lock all of it down — Part 10: Security and RBAC covers Role-Based Access Control (RBAC), ServiceAccounts, and the principle of least privilege. For the full StatefulSet field reference, the official docs are excellent: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/statefulset/. The whole series lives at /series/kubernetes-cookbook.

data belonging to web-1

Recipe 3: Orderly scaling

web-1   1/1     Running   0          20m
web-2   1/1     Running   0          20m
web-3   1/1     Running   0          6s
web-4   0/1     Pending   0          2s

web-4 does not even start until web-3 is Running and Ready. Now scale back down and watch the reverse:

kubectl scale statefulset web --replicas=3
kubectl get pods -l app=nginx -w

web-4 terminates first, fully, before web-3 is touched. Lowest ordinals are the last to die.

How it works: The default behavior is called OrderedReady. A Pod with ordinal N is only created after N-1 is ready, and Pods are terminated in reverse ordinal order. Variations:

Recipe 4: Careful updates with partitions

Problem: You want to roll out a new image slowly, canarying it on one replica before touching the rest.

StatefulSet rolling updates go from the highest ordinal down: web-2 updates first, then web-1, then web-0. The partition field lets you stop partway. Any Pod with an ordinal greater than or equal to the partition gets updated; the rest stay on the old version.

kubectl patch statefulset web --type='json' -p='[
  {"op": "replace", "path": "/spec/updateStrategy/rollingUpdate/partition", "value": 2},
  {"op": "replace", "path": "/spec/template/spec/containers/0/image", "value": "nginx:1.29"}

Delete web-2 to trigger its update (the controller only recreates a Pod above the partition when it is deleted or restarted):

kubectl get pod web-2 -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].image}'

nginx:1.29

Only web-2 moved. If the new version looks healthy, lower the partition to let the rest update:

kubectl patch statefulset web --type='json' \
  -p='[{"op": "replace", "path": "/spec/updateStrategy/rollingUpdate/partition", "value": 0}]'

How it works: With partition 2, the controller treats ordinals 0 and 1 as fenced off. It updates web-2, waits for it to be Ready, and stops. Setting the partition back to 0 resumes the normal ordered rollout. This gives you a built-in canary: the least important replica (by convention, the highest ordinal) takes the risk first. Two other strategies exist for updateStrategy.type: OnDelete, which never touches a Pod until you delete it yourself (full manual control), and the default RollingUpdate you just used.

Recipe 5: The cleanup gotcha

Problem: You are done with the StatefulSet, so you delete it — and your data silently survives.

kubectl delete statefulset web
kubectl delete service nginx
kubectl get pvc

NAME           STATUS   CAPACITY   AGE
data-web-0     Bound    100Mi      1h
data-web-1     Bound    100Mi      1h
data-web-2     Bound    100Mi      1h

The PVCs are still there. This is deliberate: Kubernetes refuses to guess whether your data is safe to destroy. If you are sure you want it gone, delete the PVCs explicitly:

(The StatefulSet labels each template-created PVC with the Pod's labels, so -l app=nginx selects them.)

How it works: A StatefulSet owns its Pods but treats PVCs as precious cargo. Deleting the controller orphans the claims rather than cascading the deletion. On a real cluster with real data, that one design choice has saved many careers.

  • Running PostgreSQL or Redis by hand with raw StatefulSets is a great way to learn, and a rough way to run production. Real databases on Kubernetes are usually managed by Operators — higher-level controllers that handle failover, backups, and upgrades for you. Look at CloudNativePG for PostgreSQL or the Bitnami Helm charts for a batteries-included start.
  • Never point two StatefulSets at the same PVC naming scheme; you will get confusing mount conflicts.

Where to go next

You now know how to run apps that remember: stable names, per-Pod storage, ordered scaling, and careful updates. In the final part of the series, you will lock all of it down — Part 10: Security and RBAC covers Role-Based Access Control (RBAC), ServiceAccounts, and the principle of least privilege. For the full StatefulSet field reference, the official docs are excellent: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/statefulset/. title: Kubernetes Cookbook Part 5: Services and Built-In Service Discovery
summary:
In Part 4 you got a Deployment running three replicas of a tiny web app. Here's the uncomfortable truth about those Pods: they are disposable. Every time one restarts, it gets a brand-new IP address, so any other app that hardcoded an IP is already broken. This part cooks the fix: a Service, which gives a changing set of Pods one stable name and one stable virtual IP, plus the cluster DNS (Domain Name System) that lets everything find everything else with zero configuration.

What you need

  • A local cluster from Part 1 (kind or minikube both work).
  • The 3-replica clinerds-demo Deployment from Part 4 running in the default namespace. Check with kubectl get deploy clinerds-demo and kubectl get pods -l app=clinerds-demo — you should see three Pods.
  • A terminal with kubectl configured to talk to that cluster.
  • No new files up front; you'll create one small YAML file per recipe.

Recipe 1: Put one stable address in front of your Pods

Problem: Your three Pods each have their own IP, and those IPs change whenever a Pod is replaced. You need one address that always reaches a healthy Pod.

Create a file called service.yaml:

apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: clinerds-demo
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: clinerds-demo
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 5678

Apply it and take a look:

kubectl apply -f service.yaml
kubectl get service clinerds-demo

NAME            TYPE        CLUSTER-IP     EXTERNAL-IP   PORT(S)   AGE
clinerds-demo   ClusterIP   10.96.173.42           80/TCP    5s

That CLUSTER-IP is only reachable from inside the cluster, so test it from a throwaway client Pod:

kubectl run netshoot --image=nicolaka/netshoot -it --rm -- bash

Inside the shell that opens:

curl clinerds-demo

You should get back hello from clinerds-demo (or whatever text you passed in Part 4). Run it a few times — different Pods answer each time. Type exit to leave; the --rm flag deletes the client Pod automatically.

How it works: A Service is three things glued together. The selector (app: clinerds-demo) continuously finds all Pods with that label, and Kubernetes records their current IPs in objects called EndpointSlices — think of them as the live guest list. The type: ClusterIP field allocates a virtual IP that exists only in the cluster's networking rules; no machine actually owns it. A small program called kube-proxy, running on every node, writes rules so traffic sent to that virtual IP gets forwarded to one of the Pod IPs from the EndpointSlice. Pod dies? It drops off the list. New Pod? It joins. The Service IP and name never change.

When it goes wrong:

  • curl hangs or refuses the connection — check that targetPort (5678) matches the port the container actually listens on, not the Service's own port (80).
  • No Pods behind the Service at all — see Recipe 5.

Recipe 2: Find Services by name with cluster DNS

Problem: You curled clinerds-demo by name in Recipe 1, but nobody told you where that name comes from or what its rules are.

Every cluster runs CoreDNS, a DNS server that watches the Kubernetes API and creates a DNS record for every Service automatically. Spin up the client Pod again:

kubectl run netshoot --image=nicolaka/netshoot -it --rm -- bash

Ask DNS who clinerds-demo is:

nslookup clinerds-demo

Server:    10.96.0.10
Address:   10.96.0.10#53

Name:   clinerds-demo.default.svc.cluster.local
Address: 10.96.173.42

Notice the full name in the answer. All three of these work from inside the Pod:

curl clinerds-demo                                  # short name, same namespace
curl clinerds-demo.default                          # name.namespace
curl clinerds-demo.default.svc.cluster.local        # the full FQDN

To see why the short name works, look at the Pod's resolver config:

cat /etc/resolv.conf

search default.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local
nameserver 10.96.0.10
options ndots:5

How it works: Kubernetes injects that resolv.conf into every Pod, pointing it at CoreDNS (10.96.0.10 is the DNS Service's own ClusterIP). The search line is the trick: when you ask for a bare name like clinerds-demo, the resolver tries it with each search suffix appended, and clinerds-demo.default.svc.cluster.local matches the record CoreDNS registered. The FQDN (fully qualified domain name) pattern is always ..svc.cluster.local. The short name only works from inside the same namespace; from another namespace you need at least name.namespace. The DNS record resolves to the Service's stable ClusterIP, so even when every Pod is replaced, the name never breaks.

Variations:

  • Need a Pod's own IP instead of the Service? Headless Services (clusterIP: None) make DNS return the Pod IPs directly. You'll meet them in Part 9.

Recipe 3: Reach the app from your laptop with NodePort

Problem: ClusterIP is cluster-internal only. You want to open the app in your own browser.

Change the Service type. Edit service.yaml so the spec looks like this:

apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: clinerds-demo
spec:
  type: NodePort
  selector:
    app: clinerds-demo
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 5678
      nodePort: 30080

kubectl apply -f service.yaml
kubectl get service clinerds-demo

NAME            TYPE       CLUSTER-IP     EXTERNAL-IP   PORT(S)       AGE
clinerds-demo   NodePort   10.96.173.42           80:30080/TCP  12m

NodePort opens port 30080 on every node's IP and forwards it to the Service. On minikube or a cloud cluster you could hit a node IP directly — but on kind, the "nodes" are Docker containers with no route from your laptop. The simple, always-works option is kubectl port-forward:

kubectl port-forward service/clinerds-demo 8080:80

Leave that running and open http://localhost:8080 in your browser. Hello from your cluster.

How it works: NodePort is not a different Service; it's ClusterIP plus one extra rule. The Service keeps its virtual IP and DNS name, and kube-proxy additionally listens on nodePort (30000–32767 by default) on every node, forwarding to the same EndpointSlice Pods. kubectl port-forward is a different mechanism entirely: your local kubectl opens a tunnel through the Kubernetes API server straight to the Service, bypassing node networking. That's why it works even on kind.

Variations:

  • minikube users: run minikube service clinerds-demo and it opens a browser with a working URL for you.
  • kind users who want real NodePort access: kind's extraPortMappings config maps node ports to your laptop, but it must be set when the cluster is created. Port-forward is the zero-setup answer.

Recipe 4: Understand what LoadBalancer really does

Problem: Every cloud tutorial says "use type: LoadBalancer." You want to know what it actually buys you before you need it.

Flip the type one more time:

apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: clinerds-demo
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  selector:
    app: clinerds-demo
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 5678

kubectl apply -f service.yaml
kubectl get service clinerds-demo

On kind, you'll see this, forever:

NAME            TYPE           CLUSTER-IP     EXTERNAL-IP   PORT(S)       AGE
clinerds-demo   LoadBalancer   10.96.173.42        80:30080/TCP  1m

How it works: LoadBalancer is NodePort plus a phone call. When the Service is created, the cloud provider's controller (built into Kubernetes on AWS, Google Cloud, Azure, and friends) provisions a real cloud load balancer, points it at your nodes' NodePorts, and writes its public address into EXTERNAL-IP. On a cloud cluster that takes a minute or two and then just works. On kind there's no cloud to call, so nothing ever fills in the address — is the expected result, not a bug. The Service still functions as ClusterIP and NodePort underneath.

Variations:

  • Homelab or bare metal? MetalLB is the standard add-on that plays the role of cloud provider and hands out IPs from a pool you define.
  • Before switching back for the next recipe, note you rarely need one LoadBalancer per app — Part 6 shows Ingress, which puts many apps behind one entry point.

Recipe 5: Debug a Service that answers with nothing

Problem: curl from the client Pod times out or refuses to connect. The Service exists, so what's missing?

Work through the checklist in order. First, does the Service have any backends?

kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=clinerds-demo

NAME                  ADDRESSTYPE   PORTS   ENDPOINTS                    AGE
clinerds-demo-x7k2p   IPv4          5678    10.244.0.8,10.244.1.4,...    15m

If that lists zero EndpointSlices or the ENDPOINTS column is empty, the selector found no Pods. Compare both sides:

kubectl get service clinerds-demo -o jsonpath='{.spec.selector}'
kubectl get pods --show-labels

The Service selector must match the Pod labels exactly. Second, read the full story:

kubectl describe service clinerds-demo

Check the Port and TargetPort lines against what your app actually listens on (5678 for http-echo). Third, confirm you're in the right namespace — Services only select Pods in their own namespace, and clinerds-demo from a Pod in namespace web resolves to clinerds-demo.web..., a different name entirely.

How it works: These are the three classic mistakes, and they cover almost every broken Service you'll meet: (1) wrong selector, so the EndpointSlice is empty; (2) wrong port/targetPort, so traffic arrives at a port nothing listens on; (3) wrong namespace, so you're querying a Service that has no Pods — or doesn't exist. endpointslices tells you what the Service sees; describe tells you what you told it to see. The diff between the two is your bug.

Where to go next

Services give every app a stable name inside the cluster — but real sites need one public entry point, hostnames, and TLS. That's Part 6: Ingress. For the full reference on everything a Service can do, read the official Kubernetes Service documentation, or head back to the series index.

title: Kubernetes Cookbook Part 10: Lock Down the API with RBAC
summary:
You can run pods, expose services, and store config now — but who is allowed to touch your cluster, and what are your pods allowed to do while they run? This final part of the series is about locking things down: we will write recipes for ServiceAccounts, Roles and Bindings, and Pod Security Standards. By the end you will have a working least-privilege setup and a short hygiene checklist you can reuse on every project.

Before the recipes, it helps to picture the path of every request to the Kubernetes API. When you run kubectl get pods, three gates stand between you and the answer:

  1. Authentication — who are you? The API server checks your identity: a client certificate, a bearer token, or a ServiceAccount token.
  2. Authorization — may you do this? The most common mode here is RBAC (Role-Based Access Control). RBAC rules say things like "user X may list pods in namespace Y."
  3. Admission control — is the object you are sending acceptable? Admission plugins can reject or mutate a request even after RBAC approves it, for example refusing a pod that wants to run as root.

Think about this like a security guard doing a threat-model exercise: who could spoof an identity, tamper with a manifest, or escalate from "read pods" to "control the node"? Every recipe below exists to shrink one of those answers. That mindset — least privilege, meaning every identity gets exactly the access it needs and nothing more — is the whole game.

What you need

  • A working local cluster from Part 1 (kind or minikube), with kubectl configured.
  • Comfort with Deployments and Pods from earlier parts.
  • Nothing else — every file below is created inline.

Recipe 1: Give the app its own ServiceAccount

Problem: Every pod that talks to the Kubernetes API needs an identity. By default, pods get the namespace's default ServiceAccount, which means you cannot tell apps apart or limit them individually.

A ServiceAccount is just a named identity for a workload inside the cluster (as opposed to a human user, which Kubernetes manages differently). Create one and run a pod with it:

kubectl create serviceaccount clinerds-demo-sa

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: clinerds-demo
spec:
  serviceAccountName: clinerds-demo-sa
  containers:
    - name: web
      image: hashicorp/http-echo:latest
      args:
        - "-text=hello from a named identity"
      ports:
        - containerPort: 5678

kubectl apply -f pod-with-sa.yaml
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod/clinerds-demo --timeout=60s

  name: default-deny-all
  namespace: default
spec:
  podSelector: {}

    - Ingress
    - Egress
