title: Kubernetes Cookbook Part 2: Pods, Labels, and Health Checks
summary:
In Part 1 you got a local cluster running with kind. Now it is time to actually run something on it. This part cooks with Pods: the smallest unit Kubernetes knows how to run. You will create single- and multi-container Pods, label and select them, give them CPU and memory budgets, and wire up the health checks that tell Kubernetes when a Pod is alive and when it is ready for traffic.

If you skipped Part 1, go set up your kind cluster first: Kubernetes Cookbook Part 1: A Local Cluster with kind. Everything below assumes kubectl talks to that cluster.

What you need

  • The kind cluster from Part 1, with kubectl configured to reach it.
  • A directory for this part's files, for example mkdir pods && cd pods.
  • Internet access so kind can pull the images hashicorp/http-echo, nginx:1.27, busybox:1.36, and curlimages/curl.

The running example for this series is clinerds-demo: the tiny hashicorp/http-echo web server that answers every HTTP request with a fixed text string on port 5678.

Recipe 1: Run a single-container Pod by the book

Problem: You know docker run. You want the Kubernetes equivalent: one container, running on the cluster, that you can inspect and poke at.

Create clinerds-demo-pod.yaml:

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: clinerds-demo
  labels:
    app: clinerds-demo
spec:
  containers:
    - name: web
      image: hashicorp/http-echo
      args:
        - "-text=hello from the clinerds demo pod"
      ports:
        - containerPort: 5678

Apply it and watch it come up:

kubectl apply -f clinerds-demo-pod.yaml
kubectl get pods -w

The -w flag watches, so you see the lifecycle in real time:

NAME           READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
clinerds-demo  0/1     Pending   0          1s
clinerds-demo  0/1     ContainerCreating   0          2s
clinerds-demo  1/1     Running   0          8s

Press Ctrl-C to stop watching. Now read the logs:

kubectl logs clinerds-demo

To prove the server answers, note the Pod's IP with kubectl get pod clinerds-demo -o wide, then call it from a throwaway debug Pod. The http-echo image is stripped down and contains no shell, so kubectl exec into it does not work — a second Pod is the reliable trick:

kubectl run curl-test --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl --restart=Never -- http://CLINERDS_DEMO_POD_IP:5678

You get back hello from the clinerds demo pod. Clean up with kubectl delete pod curl-test if anything lingered, but keep clinerds-demo running — later recipes reuse it.

How it works: A Pod is a wrapper around one or more containers that always run together on the same machine. You never say "run this on node X"; you describe the Pod and the Kubernetes scheduler picks a node for you. Pending means the scheduler is deciding or the image is still downloading, ContainerCreating means the node is setting up the container, and Running means your process is up. kubectl logs streams the container's standard output, exactly like docker logs.

When it goes wrong:

  • ImagePullBackOff in kubectl get pods means the image name or tag is wrong, or the node cannot reach the registry.
  • CrashLoopBackOff means the container starts and immediately exits. Check kubectl logs clinerds-demo for the error.

Recipe 2: Run a two-container Pod that shares data

Problem: You want nginx to serve a small HTML file, and you want a second container to keep that file fresh without rebuilding any image.

Containers in one Pod share two things: the network and (if you ask for it) volumes. This recipe uses both. Create web-with-sidecar.yaml:

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: web-with-sidecar
  labels:
    app: web-with-sidecar
spec:
  volumes:
    - name: content
      emptyDir: {}
  containers:
    - name: nginx
      image: nginx:1.27
      ports:
        - containerPort: 80
      volumeMounts:
        - name: content
          mountPath: /usr/share/nginx/html
    - name: writer
      image: busybox:1.36
      volumeMounts:
        - name: content
          mountPath: /content
      command:
        - sh
        - -c
        - |
          while true; do
            echo "
updated at $(date)
" > /content/index.html
            sleep 10
          done

kubectl apply -f web-with-sidecar.yaml
kubectl get pod web-with-sidecar

Note READY 2/2 — two containers, one Pod. Now verify the sharing from inside the Pod. busybox has a shell and wget, so kubectl exec works here if you pick the container with -c:

kubectl exec web-with-sidecar -c writer -- wget -qO- localhost:80

Run it again ten seconds later and the timestamp in the HTML has changed.

How it works: All containers in a Pod share one network namespace — one IP address, one set of ports. That is why the writer container can reach nginx as plain localhost:80: to it, nginx is literally a local process. The emptyDir volume is an empty directory Kubernetes creates when the Pod lands on a node, mounted into both containers at different paths (/content for the writer, /usr/share/nginx/html for nginx). The writer's loop overwrites index.html every 10 seconds, and nginx serves the new file immediately. One caveat: emptyDir lives and dies with the Pod. Delete the Pod and the data is gone — Part 8 covers storage that survives.

Variations:

  • Two containers in a Pod that both try to bind port 80 will fail, because the network namespace is shared. Give each container its own port.
  • kubectl logs web-with-sidecar -c writer shows one container's logs; without -c, kubectl refuses when a Pod has more than one container.

Recipe 3: Organize Pods with labels and selectors

Problem: Your cluster is filling up with Pods and you need to find, group, and act on them by role, not by random name.

Labels are key/value stickers you put on objects. The Pods from Recipes 1 and 2 already carry an app label. Add a second demo Pod with more labels, labeled-pod.yaml:

apiVersion: v1

  name: broken-liveness

      args:
        - "-text=i keep getting restarted"

        - containerPort: 5678

          path: /
          port: 8080
        periodSeconds: 5

NAME              READY   STATUS    RESTARTS      AGE
broken-liveness   1/1     Running   3 (21s ago)   2m

Warning  Unhealthy  ...  Liveness probe failed: Get "http://10.244.0.9:8080/": dial tcp ...: connect: connection refused
Normal   Killing    ...  Container web failed liveness probe, will be restarted

How it works: A probe is a health check the kubelet (the Kubernetes agent on each node) runs against your container: an HTTP GET, a TCP connect, or a command. A liveness probe answers "is this container stuck?" Fail it enough times and the kubelet restarts the container — that is the RESTARTS counter going up. A readiness probe answers "should this Pod receive traffic right now?" Fail it and the Pod is pulled out of every Service's rotation (you will see that in Part 5) but left running — no restart, because the fix might just be time. initialDelaySeconds gives a slow app room to boot before the checks start. title: Kubernetes Cookbook Part 3: Organize Clusters with Namespaces
summary:
So far in this series you have a local cluster and you know how to run Pods on it. Everything you created landed in the same big shared room. This part teaches you how to put up walls: Kubernetes namespaces let you split one physical cluster into many virtual ones, aim kubectl at the room you care about, and stop any single team from eating the whole buffet.

What you need

  • A working local cluster from Part 1 (kind or minikube) and kubectl pointed at it.
  • Comfort with creating Pods from Part 2.
  • About 20 minutes and nothing to install.

Recipe 1: Meet the built-in namespaces

Problem: You keep hearing about "namespaces" and want to know what already exists in a fresh cluster before you create your own.

Ask the cluster to list them:

kubectl get namespaces

NAME              STATUS   AGE
default           Active   4d
kube-node-lease   Active   4d
kube-public       Active   4d
kube-system       Active   4d

(kubectl get ns is the short form and does the same thing.)

How it works: A namespace is a scope for names and for API objects. Two Pods can both be called clinerds-demo as long as they live in different namespaces. The four you see above come with every cluster:

  • default is where your objects go when you don't say otherwise. Everything you made in Parts 1 and 2 lives here.
  • kube-system holds the cluster's own machinery: the DNS server, the network plugin, and so on. Look, but don't deploy your apps here.
  • kube-public is readable by everyone, even unauthenticated clients. It's mostly used for cluster discovery info and you can ignore it.
  • kube-node-lease stores small "lease" heartbeat objects that each node renews so the control plane can tell quickly when a node has died.

One caveat worth burning into memory: namespaces are not a hard security boundary by themselves. By default, a Pod in one namespace can still open network connections to Pods in every other namespace, and anyone with cluster-wide kubectl access sees everything. Namespaces give you organization and a place to hang policies. The actual locks — network policies and role-based access control (RBAC) — come later in this series, especially in Part 10.

Recipe 2: Create dev and prod lanes and run the same app in both

Problem: You want to test changes without touching the "production" copy of your app, but you only have one cluster.

Create two namespaces, one for each lane:

kubectl create namespace cookbook-dev
kubectl create namespace cookbook-prod

Now save the series demo app as clinerds-demo-pod.yaml:

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: clinerds-demo
spec:
  containers:
    - name: clinerds-demo
      image: hashicorp/http-echo
      args:
        - "-text=hello from the cookbook"
      ports:
        - containerPort: 5678

Apply the exact same file into both namespaces:

kubectl apply -f clinerds-demo-pod.yaml -n cookbook-dev
kubectl apply -f clinerds-demo-pod.yaml -n cookbook-prod

The -n flag tells kubectl which namespace to work in. Check one lane:

kubectl get all -n cookbook-dev

NAME                READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
pod/clinerds-demo   1/1     Running   0          25s

Now sweep the whole cluster at once:

kubectl get pods --all-namespaces

NAMESPACE       NAME                                READY   STATUS    AGE
cookbook-dev    clinerds-demo                       1/1     Running   40s
cookbook-prod   clinerds-demo                       1/1     Running   40s
kube-system     coredns-76f75df574-abcde            1/1     Running   4d

How it works: Both Pods are named clinerds-demo and nothing collides, because object names only have to be unique within a namespace. Think of namespaces as folders: two folders can each contain a file with the same name. --all-namespaces (short form -A) lifts the folder filter and shows you everything, which is great for "where did that thing go?" moments.

Peeking ahead: Namespaces also show up in DNS. Once an app has a Service, other Pods can reach it at service-name.namespace-name.svc.cluster.local, so dev and prod copies are addressable side by side. Part 5 serves the full story on Services and DNS.

Recipe 3: Stop typing -n on every command

Problem: You're doing all your work in cookbook-dev today and adding -n cookbook-dev to every command is getting old.

Your kubectl configuration (usually ~/.kube/config) holds a context: the bundle of "which cluster, which user, which namespace" that every command uses. Set the namespace on your current context:

kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=cookbook-dev

Verify it stuck:

kubectl config view --minify | grep namespace

    namespace: cookbook-dev

Now plain commands default to that lane:

kubectl get pods

NAME            READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
clinerds-demo   1/1     Running   0          5m

No -n needed. When you're done, switch back to the cluster-wide default:

kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=default

How it works: --current edits the context you're actively using instead of creating a new one. Every later command reads that namespace field unless you override it with an explicit -n. The setting lives in your local kubeconfig file, so it only affects your machine — it changes nothing on the cluster itself.

Variations:

  • The community tool kubens (installed alongside kubectx) makes this a one-word command: kubens cookbook-dev. Handy if you switch lanes fifty times a day.
  • You can also see the active namespace quickly with kubectl config view --minify -o jsonpath='{..namespace}'.

Recipe 4: Put a ResourceQuota on the dev buffet

Problem: The dev lane is for experiments, but one forgotten experiment shouldn't be allowed to eat the whole cluster's CPU and memory.

A ResourceQuota is a per-namespace budget. Save this as cookbook-dev-quota.yaml:

apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: cookbook-dev-quota
  namespace: cookbook-dev
spec:
  hard:
    pods: "3"
    requests.cpu: "500m"
    requests.memory: "512Mi"

kubectl apply -f cookbook-dev-quota.yaml

Make sure you're still targeting cookbook-dev from Recipe 3, then create a couple of Pods that each request 100 millicores (a millicore is one-thousandth of a CPU) and 64 mebibytes:

kubectl run demo-2 --image=hashicorp/http-echo --requests="cpu=100m,memory=64Mi" -- -text=two
kubectl run demo-3 --image=hashicorp/http-echo --requests="cpu=100m,memory=64Mi" -- -text=three

That's three Pods — the budget is full. Try a fourth:

kubectl run demo-4 --image=hashicorp/http-echo --requests="cpu=100m,memory=64Mi" -- -text=four

Error from server (Forbidden): pods "demo-4" is forbidden:
exceeded quota: cookbook-dev-quota, requested: pods=1, used: pods=3, limited: pods=3

Check the running tab any time:

kubectl describe quota cookbook-dev-quota -n cookbook-dev

Name:            cookbook-dev-quota
Namespace:       cookbook-dev
Resource         Used   Hard
--------         ----   ----
pods             3      3
requests.cpu     200m   500m

kube-system       Active   4d

title: Kubernetes Cookbook Part 1: A Local Cluster You Can Break
summary:
Every cook needs a kitchen, and before we run a single real Kubernetes recipe, we need a cluster we can afford to break. This first part of the series builds that kitchen: a throwaway cluster running on your own laptop with kind, the kubectl command-line tool to talk to it, and your very first Pod serving an HTTP response. By the end, you will be able to spin the whole thing up, wreck it, delete it, and rebuild it in under a minute — which is exactly the confidence you need for everything that follows.

What you need

The ingredients list for this entire part is short:

  • Docker Desktop (macOS or Windows) or Docker Engine (Linux) installed and running. kind stands for "Kubernetes in Docker," so Docker is the only real prerequisite. Check it with docker version — if that prints a client and server version, you are good.
  • About 15 minutes and a comfort with copy-pasting terminal commands.

Everything else — kubectl, kind, the cluster itself — we install fresh below.

Recipe 1: Install kubectl and kind

Problem: You need two tools before anything else works: kubectl, the command-line client that talks to every Kubernetes cluster, and kind, which builds a local cluster out of Docker containers.

On Linux, download both as single static binaries:

# kubectl — pin a recent stable version or fetch the latest one
curl -LO "https://dl.k8s.io/release/$(curl -Ls https://dl.k8s.io/release/stable.txt)/bin/linux/amd64/kubectl"
sudo install -o root -g root -m 0755 kubectl /usr/local/bin/kubectl

# kind — single binary, same idea
curl -Lo ./kind "https://kind.sigs.k8s.io/dl/latest/kind-linux-amd64"
sudo install -o root -g root -m 0755 kind /usr/local/bin/kind

On macOS, Homebrew does it in two lines:

brew install kubectl
brew install kind

Now verify both installations:

kubectl version --client
kind version

Client Version: v1.31.2
Kustomize Version: v5.4.2

kind v0.26.0 go1.23.4 darwin/arm64

kubectl version --client deliberately asks for only the client version — there is no cluster yet, so asking for the server version would fail.

How it works: kubectl is a single self-contained binary that speaks the Kubernetes REST API. It does not care where the cluster lives — your laptop, a cloud, a data center — as long as it has credentials. kind is a tiny wrapper that bootstraps a whole Kubernetes cluster inside one or more Docker containers on your machine, which is why it is fast, free, and disposable.

Variations:

  • Prefer a virtual machine over Docker containers? minikube (brew install minikube, or a binary from minikube.sigs.k8s.io) is the other popular local cluster. Every recipe in this series works on minikube too; just swap kind create cluster --name cookbook for minikube start -p cookbook.
  • On Windows, use Docker Desktop plus winget install -e --id Kubernetes.kubectl and winget install -e --id derailed.k9s-style installs, or grab the kind binary from its GitHub releases page.

Recipe 2: Create the playground

Problem: The tools are installed, but there is no cluster to talk to yet. Time to build one.

kind create cluster --name cookbook

Creating cluster "cookbook" ...
 ✓ Ensuring node image (kindest/node:v1.31.x)
 ✓ Preparing nodes
 ✓ Writing configuration
 ✓ Starting control-plane
 ✓ Installing CNI
 ✓ Installing StorageClass
Set kubectl context to "kind-cookbook"

Wait about 30-60 seconds, then confirm the cluster answers:

kubectl cluster-info
kubectl get nodes

Kubernetes control plane is running at https://127.0.0.1:51234

NAME                     STATUS   ROLES           AGE   VERSION
cookbook-control-plane   Ready    control-plane   90s   v1.31.2

kind also quietly updated your kubeconfig — the file at ~/.kube/config that stores cluster addresses and credentials, organized into named contexts. Look at it:

kubectl config get-contexts
kubectl config current-context

CURRENT   NAME           CLUSTER        AUTHINFO       NAMESPACE
*         kind-cookbook  kind-cookbook  kind-cookbook

How it works: A Kubernetes cluster has two kinds of machines. The control plane is the brain: it stores the desired state of everything, schedules work, and answers the API that kubectl calls. Worker nodes are the muscle: they actually run your containers. In this kind cluster both roles live in one Docker container called cookbook-control-plane (that's the "ROLES: control-plane" above) — perfect for learning, never for production. The most important idea to absorb already: Kubernetes is declarative. You do not tell it how to do things step by step; you describe the state you want ("run one copy of this image") and the control plane continuously works to make reality match. Every recipe in this series is just a different way of describing a desired state.

When it goes wrong:

  • docker: permission denied — your Linux user is not in the docker group. Run sudo usermod -aG docker $USER and log back in.
  • Port already in use — kind maps the API server to a random local port, but if you have several kind clusters, check docker ps and kind delete cluster --name .

Recipe 3: Run your first Pod imperatively

Problem: A running cluster with nothing on it is boring. Let's start the smallest unit Kubernetes runs — a Pod — with a single command, and actually reach it over HTTP.

kubectl run hello --image=hashicorp/http-echo -- -text="hello from clinerds"

pod/hello created

kubectl run creates a Pod named hello from the tiny hashicorp/http-echo image, which replies to every HTTP request with the text you pass it. One quirk: http-echo listens on port 5678 inside the container, not 80.

Check it is alive:

kubectl get pods

NAME    READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
hello   1/1     Running   0          20s

Now reach it. Pods get internal cluster IPs that are not routable from your laptop, so use kubectl port-forward to tunnel a local port into the Pod:

kubectl port-forward pod/hello 8080:5678

Leave that running, open a second terminal, and:

curl localhost:8080

hello from clinerds

Ctrl+C stops the port-forward; the Pod keeps running.

How it works: A Pod is one or more containers that share a network and get scheduled together — the atom of Kubernetes. Every Pod gets its own IP address, but only inside the cluster's private network. port-forward is a debugging bridge: kubectl opens a tunnel through the API server straight to your Pod, forwarding localhost:8080 to the container's port 5678. It is not how real traffic reaches apps (that is Services, coming in Part 5), but it is the fastest way to prove a Pod works.

Recipe 4: Same Pod, the declarative way

Problem: kubectl run worked, but one-off commands are impossible to review, version, or repeat. Real Kubernetes work happens in YAML files.

Delete the imperative Pod and write a manifest instead:

kubectl delete pod hello

Create a file named hello-pod.yaml:

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: hello
  labels:
    app: hello
spec:
  containers:
    - name: echo
      image: hashicorp/http-echo
      args: ["-text=hello from clinerds"]
      ports:
        - containerPort: 5678

Apply it and watch:

kubectl apply -f hello-pod.yaml
kubectl get pods
kubectl describe pod hello

pod/hello created

NAME    READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
hello   1/1     Running   0          10s

kubectl describe prints the Pod's full story — image, state, IP, and the Events section at the bottom, which is the first place to look when anything misbehaves.

Clean up with the same file:

kubectl delete -f hello-pod.yaml

How it works: kubectl apply sends the manifest to the API server, which stores it as the desired state and starts making it real. The manifest has four parts you will see in every Kubernetes file: apiVersion and kind say what the object is, metadata names it and attaches labels (key-value tags used for selecting things later), and spec is the desired state itself. YAML beats imperative commands for three reasons: the file is reviewable in git, apply is idempotent (run it twice, nothing changes the second time), and the file is the documentation of what should be running. From Part 2 onward, this series is YAML-only.

Recipe 5: The kubectl survival kit, then burn it all down

Problem: You will live in kubectl for the rest of this series. Learn the five commands that answer 90% of questions, then prove the playground is disposable by deleting the entire cluster.

Recreate a Pod so we have something to poke at (kubectl apply -f hello-pod.yaml again), then run the survival kit:

# What exists?
kubectl get pods

# More columns: which node, which IP
kubectl get pods -o wide

# The full object, exactly as the API server stores it
kubectl get pod hello -o yaml

# Why is it in this state? Events live here.
kubectl describe pod hello

# What did the container print?
kubectl logs hello

# What fields does a Pod spec even have? Built-in docs.
kubectl explain pod.spec.containers

kubectl explain is the quiet superpower: it works offline, for every resource type and field, and saves you a trip to the docs. Try kubectl explain pod.spec --recursive | less to see the whole tree.

Now the finale — destroy the kitchen:

kind delete cluster --name cookbook
kubectl get nodes

Deleting cluster "cookbook" ...

The connection to the server 127.0.0.1:51234 was refused

Everything — the cluster, the Pod, the state — is gone. And getting it all back is one command:

kind create cluster --name cookbook

How it works: kind delete cluster removes the Docker containers that were the cluster; there is no hidden state anywhere else. This is the whole point of the local playground: the cost of a mistake is kind delete plus 60 seconds. Treat experiments as free, because they are.

When it goes wrong:

  • kubectl hangs or refuses connections after a laptop sleep — kind clusters occasionally need docker start cookbook-control-plane after Docker restarts.
  • kubectl config get-contexts still lists a dead cluster — harmless, but clean it with kubectl config delete-context kind-cookbook.

Where to go next

You now have a cluster you can break without consequences, the two tools every Kubernetes recipe needs, and one Pod under your belt. In Part 2: Pods, we take Pods seriously — multi-container Pods, health probes, and resource limits. The full series lives at Kubernetes Cookbook, and if you want to go beyond a local sandbox someday, the official cluster setup docs cover every flavor from minikube to managed cloud.

title: Kubernetes Cookbook Part 6: Ingress, One Front Door for Every App
summary:
In Part 5 you gave every app a stable address with a Service. That works, but it leaves you with one exposed NodePort per app and a pile of random high port numbers nobody can remember. This part fixes that: you will put a single front door in front of all your apps with an Ingress, route traffic by path and by hostname, and finish by locking the door with TLS (Transport Layer Security, the encryption behind HTTPS).

What you need

  • Docker, kind, and kubectl installed (from Part 1).
  • Comfort with Pods and Services from Part 2 and Part 5.
  • A terminal where you can edit /etc/hosts (sudo access).
  • curl and openssl, which ship with macOS and most Linux distributions.

One important note up front: Ingress needs the cluster to accept traffic on ports 80 and 443. A plain kind create cluster does not forward those, so this part starts by recreating the cluster with the right port mappings.

Recipe 1: Install a front door (the ingress controller)

Problem: You have three apps and three Services of type NodePort, so users must remember localhost:31234, localhost:30877, and so on. You want one normal entry point on port 80.

Here is the key distinction that trips up every beginner: an Ingress resource is just a set of routing rules. It does nothing by itself. You also need an ingress controller — a real proxy running in the cluster that reads those rules and enforces them. We will use ingress-nginx, the controller maintained by the Kubernetes project, built on the NGINX web server.

First, delete your old cluster and create one that forwards ports 80 and 443 from your machine into the kind node:

kind delete cluster --name clinerds

Create a file named kind-ingress.yaml:

kind: Cluster
apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
nodes:
  - role: control-plane
    extraPortMappings:
      - containerPort: 80
        hostPort: 80
        protocol: TCP
      - containerPort: 443
        hostPort: 443
        protocol: TCP

kind create cluster --name clinerds --config kind-ingress.yaml

Now install the ingress-nginx controller using the manifest the project publishes specifically for kind:

kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes/ingress-nginx/main/deploy/static/provider/kind/deploy.yaml

This creates a namespace called ingress-nginx with the controller inside it. Wait until the controller Pod is ready before doing anything else:

  --for=condition=ready pod \
  --selector=app.kubernetes.io/component=controller \
  --timeout=120s

How it works: The extraPortMappings tell kind to forward port 80 and 443 on your laptop to the same ports on the cluster's node container. The ingress-nginx controller runs as a Pod on that node and binds those ports. When you later create Ingress resources, the controller watches them, translates each rule into NGINX configuration, and reloads itself. So the data flow is: your browser hits localhost:80, kind forwards it to the controller, and the controller looks up its rules to decide which Service gets the request.

  • On minikube, skip the config file entirely: minikube addons enable ingress installs the same controller, and minikube tunnel (in a separate terminal) exposes it.

Recipe 2: Route by path

Problem: Two small apps should live behind the same address, with /one going to the first and /two to the second.

Deploy two copies of our series demo app, each returning different text, plus a ClusterIP Service for each. Save as two-apps.yaml:

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: app-one
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: app-one

    metadata:
      labels:
        app: app-one
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: hashicorp/http-echo
          args:
            - "-text=hello from app one"

            - containerPort: 5678
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: app-one
spec:

    app: app-one
  ports:
    - port: 80

---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: app-two
spec:
  replicas: 1

    matchLabels:

    metadata:
      labels:
        app: app-two

      containers:
        - name: web

            - "-text=hello from app two"

            - containerPort: 5678

spec:

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: clinerds-demo
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx

            backend:

                name: app-one
                port:

Problem: Traffic to one.clinerds.local is plain HTTP. You want HTTPS with a certificate, without touching the apps at all.

  -subj "/CN=one.clinerds.local" \
  -addext "subjectAltName=DNS:one.clinerds.local"

metadata:
  name: clinerds-demo
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  tls:
    - hosts:
        - one.clinerds.local
      secretName: one-clinerds-tls
  rules:
    - host: one.clinerds.local
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: app-one
                port:
                  number: 80

Apply it and call the HTTPS endpoint with -v (verbose) and -k (accept the self-signed certificate):

kubectl apply -f ingress-hosts.yaml
curl -vk https://one.clinerds.local

In the verbose output you can watch the handshake happen at the controller:

*   Trying 127.0.0.1:443...
* SSL connection using TLSv1.3
* Server certificate:
*  subject: CN=one.clinerds.local
> GET / HTTP/1.1
> Host: one.clinerds.local
< HTTP/1.1 200 OK
hello from app one

How it works: This is TLS termination at the edge. The controller holds the certificate, performs the encrypted handshake with the client, decrypts the request, applies its routing rules, and forwards plain HTTP to your Pod inside the cluster network. Your app never sees a certificate, which is why the same unmodified http-echo container now serves HTTPS. The tls block ties a hostname to a Secret; when the handshake for one.clinerds.local arrives, the controller presents that certificate.

Variations:

  • For real, browser-trusted certificates, look at cert-manager. It automates issuing and renewing certificates (for example from Let's Encrypt) and writes them into TLS Secrets just like the one you created by hand.
  • Self-signed certs are fine for local development, but any fleet-wide rollout should come from cert-manager so renewals never become a 3 a.m. pager event.

Recipe 5: Debug the front door

Problem: You applied an Ingress and get an error page. Where do you even look?

Three places, in this order.

First, ask Kubernetes what it thinks of the rules:

kubectl describe ingress clinerds-demo

Name:             clinerds-demo
Ingress Class:    nginx
Rules:
  Host                 Path  Backends
  ----                 ----  --------
  one.clinerds.local
                       /   app-one:80 (10.244.0.12:5678)
Events:
  Type    Reason  Age   Message
  ----    ------  ----  -------
  Normal  Sync    12s   Scheduled for sync

The Events section tells you whether a controller accepted the Ingress. No Sync event at all is your first clue that no controller is watching this object — almost always a class mismatch.

Second, read the controller's own logs:

kubectl logs -n ingress-nginx -l app.kubernetes.io/component=controller --tail=20

Every request the controller handles shows up here with the status code it returned, which lets you see whether traffic even reached the door.

Third, interpret the status code:

  • 404 from NGINX means the controller answered but no rule matched. Check the Host header (did you edit /etc/hosts?), the path, and pathType.
  • 502 Bad Gateway means a rule matched but the backend is broken: wrong Service name, wrong port, or zero ready Pods behind the Service. Check with kubectl get endpoints app-one — an empty list means the Service selector matches nothing.
  • Nothing at all (connection refused) means the controller itself is down or the port mapping is missing. Revisit Recipe 1.

How it works: Debugging Ingress is just untangling three layers: the client (is the hostname right?), the controller (did it sync the rules?), and the backend (does the Service resolve to healthy Pod IPs?). The classic beginner trap is ingressClassName: older tutorials omit it, but if your cluster has several controllers — or none marked as default — a classless Ingress is silently ignored. Always set it explicitly.

Where to go next

Your apps now have one clean, encrypted front door. In Part 7 you will stop baking configuration like -text=... into your manifests and learn how ConfigMaps and Secrets feed settings and sensitive values into Pods. For the full reference on rule types and controllers, see the official Kubernetes Ingress documentation. All parts of the series live at /series/kubernetes-cookbook.

title: How DevSecOps Improves Security in Custom Software Development
summary:
It is no secret that companies across various industries are looking to deploy applications quicker and quicker. Why, you ask. Well that would be to gain a competitive edge. In order to keep up with the demands of the modern market, more and more companies are deploying their applications with the help of cloud computing. And there is certainly no denying that cloud based applications bring forth a world of benefits. But it can also cause a jump in the number of attack elements your business is exposed to.

This is especially true if you still use traditional methods to secure your software. Having your app security team go through each application risks making you fall behind the competition. Thankfully, a handy solution to these obstacles exists: All you need to do is implement new ways of thinking when it comes to software development and IT security.

I will explain the security must be a continuous consideration across the development process in order for your apps to remain secure. This is where DevSecOps comes into play. This framework is engineered to empower your team to identify code vulnerabilities and enforce access controls. And all this is done without slowing down release schedules, of course.

In this blog, I will discuss DevSecOps, i.e. what it is and its benefits for safeguarding your digital assets while still maintaining high development pace.

DevSecOps Fundamentals

The term refers to a software development strategy. It brings together security practices into each stage of the software development lifecycle. As you can see, it differs from traditional models wherein security is simply a final check before release. Instead DevSecOps integrates automated security testing, vulnerability scanning, etc. straight into CI/CD pipelines. This is also conducive to collaboration between developers, IT, and security teams. And most importantly, DevSecOps ensures security flaws are found and remediated early in the development process.

Top Benefits of DevSecOps for Building Custom Software

  • Reduced security incidents: The use of this framework means automated security tools are embedded straight into the early coding stages. And when you do find and fix vulnerabilities such as SQL injection and broken authentication during the development process, you can prevent insecure code from making its way into production. As you can imagine, such a proactive approach greatly reduces the overall volume of active security breaches and operational incidents.
  • Decreased time spends on compliance audits: The DevSecOps approach also involves the automation of security testing reports, code review logs, etc. Since measures such as security policies and compliance guardrails are integrated and recorded as code, security and compliance teams don't have to manually gather evidence or reconstruct change logs from a handful of different systems. So when a regulatory audits does happen, you have all the documentation ready to go.
  • Quicker remediation of zero-day vulnerabilities: Yet another benefit of this approach is the use of automated dependency scanning tools. These solutions continuously analyze third-party libraries and open-source packages against global vulnerability databases. When a new zero-day exploit comes to the fore, DevSecOps will instantly get to work. It will scan all active codebases and repositories to find where the vulnerable component is used. This immediate visibility helps development teams to patch or update the compromised dependency extremely quickly.
  • Faster deployments: DevSecOps does away with manual security testing models. In their stead, it brings to the table automated security tests which run in parallel with code development. Since security is being continuously validated inside the CI/CD pipeline, the approved code can move from development to production automatically.

Ready to embrace DevSecOps, then? Then you must first start looking for a trusted software development services company.

title: Kubernetes Cookbook Part 4: Deployments, Rollouts, and Rollbacks
summary:
In Part 3 you saw how namespaces keep a cluster tidy, and back in Part 2 you ran raw Pods by hand. Running Pods by hand is fine for learning, but it falls apart fast in real life: nobody restarts a crashed Pod at 3 a.m., and nobody wants downtime just to ship new code. In this part you will cook with Deployments, the workload object that manages replicas, heals itself, rolls out updates without downtime, and keeps a one-command undo button in your pocket.

What you need

  • A local cluster from Part 1 (kind or minikube both work).
  • kubectl configured to talk to it (kubectl get nodes should answer).
  • Comfort with Pods from Part 2. That is all — every file below is created from scratch.

Recipe 1: Serve your first Deployment

Problem: You want three copies of your demo app running at all times, managed as one unit, not three loose Pods you babysit.

Create a file named deployment.yaml:

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: clinerds-demo
  labels:
    app: clinerds-demo
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: clinerds-demo
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: clinerds-demo
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: hashicorp/http-echo
          args:
            - "-text=hello from the deployment"
          ports:
            - containerPort: 5678

Apply it and look at everything it created:

kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
kubectl get deploy,rs,pods

NAME                            READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE   AGE
deployment.apps/clinerds-demo   3/3     3            3           20s

NAME                                       DESIRED   CURRENT   READY   AGE
replicaset.apps/clinerds-demo-7d9c4f8b5    3         3         3       20s

NAME                                 READY   STATUS    RUNNING   AGE
pod/clinerds-demo-7d9c4f8b5-2xkpt    1/1     Running   0         20s
pod/clinerds-demo-7d9c4f8b5-8qmzv    1/1     Running   0         20s
pod/clinerds-demo-7d9c4f8b5-wj6ln    1/1     Running   0         20s

Notice you only wrote one YAML file, but three kinds of objects appeared. Check one Pod actually serves traffic:

kubectl port-forward deployment/clinerds-demo 8080:5678
# in another terminal:
curl localhost:8080

How it works: A Deployment does not run containers directly. It works through a chain: Deployment creates a ReplicaSet, and the ReplicaSet creates the Pods. A ReplicaSet is a simple bookkeeping object whose only job is "keep N Pods with these labels alive." The Deployment's selector.matchLabels must match the labels in template.metadata.labels — that label is the string tying the whole chain together. Why the extra layer? Because the ReplicaSet is pinned to an exact Pod template. When you change the template later, the Deployment makes a new ReplicaSet, and the old one stays behind as a snapshot. That is what makes rollouts and rollbacks possible in Recipes 4 and 5. Also note the Pod names: ReplicaSet hash plus a random suffix. Never hardcode a Pod name anywhere — they are disposable by design.

Recipe 2: Prove self-healing

Problem: You want to know that when a Pod dies — crash, node hiccup, or a clumsy kubectl delete — your app keeps running without you.

Watch the Pods in one terminal:

kubectl get pods -w

In another terminal, delete one of them (use a real name from your cluster):

kubectl delete pod clinerds-demo-7d9c4f8b5-2xkpt

In the watching terminal you will see the old Pod go Terminating and a brand new Pod — with a different random suffix — appear and reach Running within seconds:

clinerds-demo-7d9c4f8b5-2xkpt   1/1   Terminating   0    5m
clinerds-demo-7d9c4f8b5-9cfrd   0/1   Pending       0    0s
clinerds-demo-7d9c4f8b5-9cfrd   1/1   Running       0    4s

How it works: Kubernetes runs a reconciliation loop. Controllers constantly compare desired state (your YAML says 3 replicas) with actual state (how many matching Pods are alive right now). The moment actual drops below desired, the ReplicaSet creates a replacement. You never asked it to — the loop just keeps pulling reality back toward your declaration. This is the big mental shift from Docker: with docker run you manage processes; with Kubernetes you declare an outcome and the cluster maintains it forever.

When it goes wrong:

  • If the new Pod stays Pending, your cluster is out of room — run kubectl describe pod and read the Events at the bottom.
  • If it flaps between Running and CrashLoopBackOff, the container itself is failing. That is app trouble, not scheduling trouble: kubectl logs is your friend.

Recipe 3: Scale the service

Problem: Traffic doubled (or you just want more headroom). You need five copies instead of three, without touching anything else.

There are two ways. The declarative way: edit deployment.yaml, change replicas: 3 to replicas: 5, and re-apply:

kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
kubectl get pods

The imperative way, straight from the command line:

kubectl scale deployment clinerds-demo --replicas=5

Either way, two new Pods appear. Scale back down with replicas: 3 and the extra Pods are terminated.

How it works: Both paths end at the same place — the replicas field on the Deployment, which the ReplicaSet treats as its target. kubectl scale is a shortcut that edits that one field on the live object; kubectl apply re-syncs the whole manifest. The loop from Recipe 2 does the rest, creating or deleting Pods until actual matches desired.

Variations:

  • Prefer the YAML route when you keep manifests in Git. kubectl scale only changes the cluster, so your file and reality drift apart — and the next kubectl apply silently scales you back.
  • Kubernetes can also scale for you. kubectl autoscale deployment clinerds-demo --min=2 --max=10 --cpu-percent=80 creates a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) that adds replicas when CPU usage climbs. Caveat: it needs metrics-server installed, which minikube ships as an addon (minikube addons enable metrics-server) but kind does not include by default. We will revisit autoscaling later in the series.

Recipe 4: Roll out an update with zero downtime

Problem: You want to ship a new version — a different message from http-echo — without visitors ever hitting a gap.

First, add a rollout strategy to deployment.yaml under spec (same level as replicas), and change the text:

spec:
  replicas: 3
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1
      maxUnavailable: 0
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: clinerds-demo
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: clinerds-demo
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: hashicorp/http-echo
          args:
            - "-text=version two is live"
          ports:
            - containerPort: 5678

Apply and watch the rollout happen:

kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
kubectl rollout status deployment clinerds-demo

Waiting for deployment "clinerds-demo" rollout to finish: 2 out of 3 new replicas have been updated...
Waiting for deployment "clinerds-demo" rollout to finish: 1 old replicas are pending termination...
deployment "clinerds-demo" successfully rolled out

While it runs, kubectl get rs shows the overlap — the old ReplicaSet draining as the new one fills:

NAME                          DESIRED   CURRENT   READY   AGE
clinerds-demo-7d9c4f8b5       1         1         1       30m
clinerds-demo-5b6f9d7c4       3         3         3       40s

How it works: Changing the Pod template produces a new template hash, so the Deployment builds a new ReplicaSet and performs a RollingUpdate: spin up new Pods, wait for each to pass its readiness, then retire old ones. The strategy block tunes the shape of that handoff. maxSurge: 1 allows one extra Pod above your replica count during the swap, and maxUnavailable: 0 forbids dropping below the full count — together they guarantee three working Pods at every moment. kubectl rollout status just blocks until the new ReplicaSet is fully up and the old one is empty, which makes it perfect for CI scripts.

Recipe 5: Roll back a bad release

Problem: Version two shipped a bug (or just the wrong message). You need to go back — fast, and ideally to a specific known-good revision.

First, make history useful. Annotate each release as you apply it:

kubectl annotate deployment clinerds-demo \
  kubernetes.io/change-cause="switch text to version two" --overwrite
kubectl rollout history deployment clinerds-demo

REVISION  CHANGE-CAUSE
1         initial release: hello from the deployment
2         switch text to version two

Now undo the release:

kubectl rollout undo deployment clinerds-demo
kubectl rollout status deployment clinerds-demo

Curl the app again and the original message is back. To jump to a specific revision instead of just "one step back":

kubectl rollout undo deployment clinerds-demo --to-revision=1

How it works: Remember those old ReplicaSets from Recipe 4? The Deployment keeps them around (scaled to zero) as frozen snapshots of previous Pod templates. rollout undo does not rebuild anything — it points the Deployment back at an older ReplicaSet and scales it back up, using the same zero-downtime rolling mechanics. change-cause annotations are what turn rollout history from a list of mysterious numbers into a changelog your future self will thank you for.

Variations:

  • kubectl rollout pause deployment clinerds-demo freezes rollouts so you can apply several changes (image, env, resources) and ship them as one batch, then kubectl rollout resume to release it all at once.
  • The number of old revisions kept is controlled by spec.revisionHistoryLimit (default 10). Lower it on noisy Deployments to keep etcd lean.

Where to go next

Your Pods now heal, scale, and update themselves — but they still get a brand new IP address every time they are replaced, and nothing stable points at them. In Part 5: Services you will give the app a permanent virtual IP and DNS name, and learn how traffic finds the right Pods. For the full field-by-field reference, the official Deployment documentation is excellent. The whole series lives at /series/kubernetes-cookbook.
